title: Scarcity: You Can't Pack Everything

sections.heading: The Backpack Problem
sections.markdown:
You're heading up into the Sawtooths for an overnight hike. Your pack holds about 40 pounds before your shoulders start filing complaints. You want a tent, a sleeping bag, a stove, water, food, a jacket, a speaker, a hammock, a camp chair, and maybe a cast-iron pan because bacon.
It won't all fit. So you choose.
That moment, standing over a pile of gear and deciding what stays home, is economics. Not stocks. Not math. **Choices.**

sections.heading: What Economics Actually Is
sections.markdown:
**Economics** is the study of how people make choices when they can't have everything they want.
It exists because of one basic fact: **scarcity**. Scarcity means our wants are unlimited, but the resources we use to satisfy them are limited. There's only so much time, money, land, water, and energy.
Scarcity is not the same as a **shortage**. A shortage is temporary: the store is out of your size this week. Scarcity is permanent. Even billionaires face it. They still only get 24 hours a day.
Economists split what people want into two piles:
- **Needs** are things you must have to survive: food, water, shelter, clothing.
- **Wants** are things that would be nice to have: the new phone, the lake trip, extra guac.
The stuff we buy comes in two types too. **Goods** are physical things you can touch, like hiking boots. **Services** are actions someone does for you, like a ski lesson or a haircut.

sections.heading: Every Choice Has a Price Tag (Even When It's Free)
sections.markdown:
When you choose one thing, you give up something else. That's a **trade-off**.
The single best thing you gave up is your **opportunity cost**. Say you have a free Saturday. You could work a shift and earn $90, hike Table Rock with friends, or sleep until noon. If you pick the hike and your next-best choice was working, your opportunity cost is the $90 you didn't earn.
Notice: the hike was "free," but it still cost you something. Economists say **there's no such thing as a free lunch.** Somebody always gives something up, even if it's just time.

sections.heading: Thinking at the Margin
sections.markdown:
Most choices aren't all-or-nothing. They're "a little more or a little less." Economists call this **marginal thinking**.
Should you study one more hour for the test? Compare the **marginal benefit** (maybe your grade goes up a few points) with the **marginal cost** (one less hour of sleep or fun). If the extra benefit is bigger than the extra cost, do it. If not, stop.
That's also why the first slice of pizza is amazing and the fifth one isn't. Each extra slice gives you less satisfaction than the one before.

sections.heading: Incentives: Why People Do What They Do
sections.markdown:
An **incentive** is anything that pushes people to act a certain way.
- **Positive incentives** reward you: a bonus for working Black Friday, a discount for buying early, extra XP for passing a quiz.
- **Negative incentives** punish you: a speeding ticket, a late fee, losing your phone for missing curfew.
When incentives change, behavior changes. If gas prices jump, people drive less and carpool more. If a store gives free ice cream with any purchase, watch how fast the line grows. Economists can predict a lot just by asking, "What's the incentive here?"

sections.heading: Rational Choices and the Big Three Questions
sections.markdown:
Economists assume people are mostly **rational**. That doesn't mean perfect. It means people try to pick the option where the benefits beat the costs, based on what they know.
Because of scarcity, every society has to answer three big questions:
1. **What** should we produce? (More trail maps or more video games?)
2. **How** should we produce it? (By hand, by machine, by robot?)
3. **For whom** should we produce it? (Who gets the stuff?)
How a country answers these questions is a big deal. You'll see different answers in Chapter 3.

sections.heading: Micro vs. Macro
sections.markdown:
Economics has two zoom levels:
- **Microeconomics** looks at individual people, families, and businesses. Should Boise Fry Company raise its prices?
- **Macroeconomics** looks at the whole economy at once: total jobs, prices, and growth across the entire country.
Same trail, two different maps. You'll use both before you reach the summit.

thinkLikeAScientist.prompt:
Your family has $300 to spend this month on "fun." Option A: a weekend at a cabin near McCall. Option B: four new video games. Option C: put it in savings for a summer road trip.
Pick one. Then explain your **opportunity cost**, name one **incentive** that pushed your choice, and describe one **marginal** decision inside your choice (for example, "one more night" or "one more game").

checklist: Scarcity = unlimited wants, limited resources. It never goes away.
Opportunity cost is the value of your next-best choice, the one you gave up.
Marginal thinking compares the extra benefit with the extra cost of one more.
Incentives (positive and negative) change how people act.
Every society must answer: what, how, and for whom to produce.

title: Resources and the Production Possibilities Curve

sections.heading: Building a Trail From Scratch
sections.markdown:
Imagine the Forest Service hands your class a job: build a new two-mile trail up a ridge outside Idaho Falls. What do you need?
Land to put it on. People to dig. Shovels, saws, and a truck. And somebody to organize the whole thing so it doesn't turn into 30 teenagers arguing over one shovel.
Congratulations, you just named the four **factors of production**.

sections.heading: The Four Factors of Production
sections.markdown:
Everything that gets made, from a potato chip to a phone, uses these four ingredients:
- **Land** means every natural resource: soil, water, trees, minerals, oil, sunlight. Idaho's farmland, rivers, and timber are all land.
- **Labor** is human work, physical or mental. The trail crew digging, a nurse at EIRMC, a coder at Micron.
- **Capital** is anything people *make* to help make other things: tools, machines, buildings, trucks. (Careful: in economics, capital does *not* mean money. Money buys capital. Capital is the shovel.)
- **Entrepreneurship** is the skill of combining the other three, taking risks, and starting something new. The person who says "let's open a rafting company on the Snake River" is the entrepreneur.
Economists also talk about **human capital**: the knowledge and skills a person gains from school, training, and experience. When you learn to weld or code, you're building your human capital. It makes your labor worth more.
Each factor earns its own reward. Land earns **rent**, labor earns **wages**, capital earns **interest**, and entrepreneurs earn **profit** (if things go well).

sections.heading: Productivity: Doing More With the Same Stuff
sections.markdown:
**Productivity** is how much you can produce with the resources you have. A trail crew with power tools gets more done per hour than one with hand shovels.
Two big ways to raise productivity:
1. **Specialization**: each person focuses on one task they're good at. One group clears brush, one digs, one builds water bars. Everyone gets faster at their part.
2. **Division of labor**: breaking a big job into small steps. Henry Ford's assembly line made cars cheap enough for regular families this way.
Better technology and more human capital raise productivity too. More productivity is how countries get richer over time.

sections.heading: The Production Possibilities Curve
sections.markdown:
Economists use a simple graph to show scarcity and trade-offs. It's called a **production possibilities curve (PPC)**, sometimes called a frontier.
Imagine a small town that can only make two things: **skis** and **fishing rods**. If it uses every worker and machine for skis, it gets 100 skis and zero rods. All rods? 80 rods, zero skis. Most of the time it picks a mix, like 60 skis and 50 rods.
Plot all the best possible combinations and you get a curve that bows outward. Here's what the curve tells you:
- **On the curve**: the town is using all its resources efficiently. To make more skis, it *must* make fewer rods. That's opportunity cost, drawn as a line.
- **Inside the curve**: resources are being wasted. Maybe workers are unemployed or a factory sits empty. The town could make more of both.
- **Outside the curve**: impossible right now. The town doesn't have enough resources or technology.

sections.heading: Why the Curve Bends
sections.markdown:
The curve bows outward because of the **law of increasing opportunity cost**. Not every resource is equally good at everything.
When the town makes its first few fishing rods, it uses the workers who are best at rods, so it gives up only a few skis. But the more rods it makes, the more it has to pull in expert ski makers who are terrible at rods. Each extra rod costs more and more skis.

sections.heading: Moving the Whole Curve
sections.markdown:
The curve can shift.
- It shifts **outward** (growth) when the town gets more resources, better technology, or more educated workers. A new factory or a faster machine lets it make more of everything.
- It shifts **inward** when resources are lost: a wildfire burns timberland, a flood wipes out a factory, or many workers move away.
This is the whole story of economic growth on one graph. Countries grow by pushing their curve outward, mostly through new capital, better technology, and stronger human capital.

thinkLikeAScientist.prompt:
A student has 6 hours on Saturday to split between **working** ($15/hour) and **studying** (each hour raises a test grade about 3 points, but only for the first 4 hours).
Sketch or describe a production possibilities curve with "Dollars earned" on one axis and "Points gained" on the other. Label one point **inside** the curve and explain what it means. Then explain what could shift this student's curve **outward**.

checklist: The four factors of production: land, labor, capital, entrepreneurship.
In economics, capital means tools and machines, not money.
Specialization and division of labor raise productivity.
On the PPC = efficient; inside = wasted resources; outside = impossible for now.
More resources, better technology, or more human capital shift the PPC outward.

title: Economic Systems: Who Decides?

sections.heading: Three Questions, Many Answers
sections.markdown:
In Chapter 1 you met the three questions every society has to answer: **what** to produce, **how** to produce it, and **for whom**.
An **economic system** is the way a society answers those questions. Think of it as the trail rules for a whole country. Some countries let each hiker pick their own route. Others have a ranger tell everyone exactly where to walk. Most do a bit of both.

sections.heading: Traditional Economies
sections.markdown:
In a **traditional economy**, people answer the three questions the way their parents and grandparents did. Customs and habits decide. If your family has always herded reindeer, you herd reindeer.
Traditional economies still exist in a few places, such as some Indigenous communities, rural villages, and herding groups around the world. They offer stability and strong community. The downside is that they change slowly and rarely adopt new technology, so living standards tend to stay where they are.

sections.heading: Command Economies
sections.markdown:
In a **command economy**, the central government makes the big decisions. Planners decide what factories make, how much they make, what things cost, and who gets them. The government usually owns most land and businesses.
The Soviet Union ran a command economy for about 70 years. Today North Korea and Cuba come closest.
**Strengths:** the government can move resources fast toward a goal, like building a military or a dam.
**Weaknesses:** planners can't possibly know what millions of people want. The Soviet Union had warehouses full of shoes nobody liked and long lines for bread. Workers had few incentives to work harder or invent something better, because they couldn't keep the rewards.

sections.heading: Market Economies
sections.markdown:
In a **market economy**, individuals and private businesses answer the three questions. People buy what they want, businesses make what sells, and prices send the signals. Nobody's in charge, yet stuff still shows up on the shelves.
The Scottish thinker **Adam Smith** explained this in *The Wealth of Nations* (1776). He said that when people pursue their own **self-interest** in a market, an "**invisible hand**" guides them to help others too. A baker doesn't bake bread to be nice. She bakes because she wants to earn money. But you still get bread.
Pure market economies, with zero government, don't really exist. That's sometimes called **laissez-faire** ("leave it alone").
**Strengths:** freedom of choice, lots of variety, and strong incentives to work and invent.
**Weaknesses:** markets don't take care of everyone. Some people can't work, some businesses pollute, and big swings between booms and busts can hurt.

sections.heading: Mixed Economies (Including Ours)
sections.markdown:
Nearly every country today is a **mixed economy**, blending market freedom with some government decisions. The real question is *how much* of each.
The United States leans strongly toward the market side. That system is called **free enterprise**, or **capitalism**. Its key features:
- **Private property**: people can own land, homes, and businesses.
- **Profit motive**: people start businesses hoping to earn money.
- **Competition**: businesses compete for customers, which pushes prices down and quality up.
- **Voluntary exchange**: buyers and sellers trade only when both think they'll be better off.
- **Consumer sovereignty**: shoppers are the "kings and queens" whose spending decides what gets made.
The U.S. government still plays roles: enforcing contracts, protecting property, providing roads and national defense, regulating safety, and running programs like Social Security.

sections.heading: Big Thinkers, Big Debates
sections.markdown:
Economic systems grew out of big ideas, and people still argue about them.
- **Adam Smith** (1700s): free markets and competition create wealth.
- **Karl Marx** (1800s): believed capitalism let factory owners take advantage of workers and predicted workers would overthrow it. His ideas inspired **socialism** (government or society owns major industries) and **communism** (a planned system where the government controls nearly all property). Countries that tried communism ended up with command economies and harsh limits on freedom.
- **John Maynard Keynes** (1900s): said government should spend more during recessions to boost the economy.
- **Friedrich Hayek** and **Milton Friedman** (1900s): warned that too much government control hurts freedom and growth, and argued for freer markets.
Today, countries like Sweden and Denmark have market economies with high taxes and large social programs. Hong Kong and Singapore became famous for very free markets. China has a command-economy past with large market reforms since 1978. Every country is somewhere on the spectrum, and voters keep debating where the line should be.

thinkLikeAScientist.prompt:
A small island of 500 people just got cut off from the world. Food is limited. Pick an economic system (traditional, command, market, or mixed) for the island.
Explain how your system answers **what, how, and for whom** to produce. Then give one real **strength** and one real **weakness** your island will face, using evidence from a real country or history.

checklist: An economic system is how a society answers what, how, and for whom.
Traditional = custom decides. Command = government decides. Market = individuals and prices decide.
Almost every country today is a mixed economy.
U.S. free enterprise: private property, profit motive, competition, voluntary exchange, consumer sovereignty.
Adam Smith's invisible hand vs. Karl Marx's critique are still debated today.

title: Demand: What Buyers Want

sections.heading: The Lift Ticket Experiment
sections.markdown:
A ski hill near you sells a day pass for $90. Plenty of people buy. Now imagine they drop it to $30. The parking lot overflows and the lift line wraps around the lodge. Push it up to $200 and the slopes are empty except for a few diehards.
Nobody had to pass a law to make that happen. People just responded to price. That's **demand** at work.

sections.heading: What Demand Means
sections.markdown:
**Demand** is how much of something people are **willing and able** to buy at each possible price. Both parts matter. You may *want* a $60,000 truck, but if you can't pay for it, that's not demand. It's a daydream.
The **law of demand** says: when the price of something goes **up**, people buy **less** of it. When the price goes **down**, people buy **more**. Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.
Why? Two reasons:
- **The income effect:** when prices rise, your money doesn't stretch as far, so you buy less.
- **The substitution effect:** when something gets pricey, you switch to something cheaper. If burgers jump to $15, you start eating more tacos.
There's also **diminishing marginal utility** (utility just means satisfaction). The first water bottle on a hot trail is priceless. The fifth? You'd only take it if it were nearly free. So people only buy more when the price drops.

sections.heading: Demand Schedules and Demand Curves
sections.markdown:
A **demand schedule** is a table showing how much people will buy at each price:
- $10 a bag of kettle corn: 20 bags
- $8: 40 bags
- $6: 60 bags
- $4: 80 bags
Draw those points on a graph with **price** on the vertical axis and **quantity** on the horizontal axis, connect them, and you get a **demand curve**. It slopes **downward** from left to right. That's the law of demand in picture form.
**Market demand** adds up what every buyer wants at each price, not just one person.

sections.heading: Moving Along vs. Shifting the Curve
sections.markdown:
This part trips people up, so slow down.
If the **price of the product itself** changes, you **move along** the same curve. That's a **change in quantity demanded**.
If **something else** changes, the whole curve **shifts**. That's a **change in demand**. Shift right = more demand at every price. Shift left = less demand at every price.

sections.heading: What Shifts Demand
sections.markdown:
Remember **"TRIBE"** for the five big shifters:
- **T**astes and preferences: a viral TikTok makes everyone want Stanley cups. Demand shifts right.
- **R**elated goods: **Substitutes** replace each other (Coke and Pepsi). If Pepsi gets cheaper, demand for Coke falls. **Complements** go together (hot dogs and buns, game consoles and games). If consoles get cheaper, demand for games rises.
- **I**ncome: more income usually raises demand for **normal goods** (restaurant meals, new clothes). For **inferior goods** (ramen, bus rides, used cars), demand can *fall* as income rises because people upgrade.
- **B**uyers: more buyers means more demand. When people move to Idaho, demand for houses goes up.
- **E**xpectations: if you think prices will jump next week, you buy now. Rumors of a gas shortage cause lines today.

sections.heading: Elasticity: How Picky Are Buyers?
sections.markdown:
**Elasticity of demand** measures how much buyers react to a price change.
- **Elastic demand:** a small price change causes a big change in how much people buy. Things with lots of substitutes, luxuries, or big-ticket items are usually elastic. Raise the price of one brand of chips and people grab another.
- **Inelastic demand:** people keep buying about the same amount even when the price changes. Necessities with few substitutes are inelastic: insulin, gasoline for your commute, electricity. When gas jumps 50 cents, you still have to get to work.
Three questions predict elasticity: Are there **substitutes**? Is it a **need or a want**? Is it a **big part of your budget**? Lots of substitutes, a want, and a big price tag mean elastic.
Businesses care a lot about this. If demand is inelastic, raising prices can bring in more money. If it's elastic, raising prices might drive customers away.

thinkLikeAScientist.prompt:
Pick something you buy often (a drink, a game, gas, a streaming service).
1. Is your demand for it **elastic or inelastic**? Use the three questions (substitutes, need vs. want, share of budget) as evidence.
2. Name one event that would **shift your demand curve right** and one that would **shift it left**, and say which TRIBE factor each one is.

checklist: Demand = willing AND able to buy at each price.
Law of demand: price up, quantity demanded down (and the reverse).
A price change moves you along the curve; other factors shift the whole curve.
TRIBE: tastes, related goods, income, buyers, expectations.
Elastic = buyers react a lot to price; inelastic = they keep buying anyway.

title: Supply: What Sellers Bring

sections.heading: The Huckleberry Hustle
sections.markdown:
Every August, people head into the hills around Sandpoint and Island Park to pick wild huckleberries. Pickers sell them for crazy prices, sometimes $50 a gallon or more.
Now picture the price jumping to $100 a gallon. What happens? Suddenly everybody's uncle has a bucket and a free weekend. More people pick, they pick longer, and they hike farther to find berries. More berries show up for sale.
That's **supply**: sellers bringing more to market when the price is worth their time.

sections.heading: What Supply Means
sections.markdown:
**Supply** is the amount of a good or service that producers are **willing and able** to sell at each possible price.
The **law of supply** says: when the price goes **up**, producers offer **more**. When the price goes **down**, they offer **less**. Price and quantity supplied move in the **same** direction.
Why? Because of incentives. A higher price means more profit, so:
- businesses already selling make more of it,
- new businesses jump in to grab some of that profit.

sections.heading: Supply Schedules and Curves
sections.markdown:
A **supply schedule** is a table of how much sellers will offer at each price:
- $2 per cup of lemonade: 10 cups
- $3: 25 cups
- $4: 40 cups
- $5: 55 cups
Graph it with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal and you get a **supply curve** that slopes **upward** from left to right. That's the opposite of a demand curve.
**Market supply** adds up what every seller will offer at each price.

sections.heading: Costs Drive Supply
sections.markdown:
Sellers decide how much to make by looking at their costs.
- **Fixed costs** stay the same no matter how much you make: rent, insurance, a loan payment on the food truck.
- **Variable costs** rise with each unit you make: ingredients, packaging, hourly wages, gas.
- **Total cost** = fixed costs + variable costs.
- **Marginal cost** is the extra cost of making one more unit.
A business keeps producing as long as the price it gets for one more unit (**marginal revenue**) is at least as big as the marginal cost. That's marginal thinking again, from Chapter 1.
At some point, adding more workers stops helping as much. Three people in a food truck work great. Ten people trip over each other. That's **diminishing marginal returns**: each extra worker adds less output than the one before.

sections.heading: Moving Along vs. Shifting
sections.markdown:
Same rule as demand:
- A change in the **good's own price** = a **movement along** the supply curve (a change in **quantity supplied**).
- A change in **anything else** = the whole curve **shifts** (a change in **supply**). Right = more supply at every price. Left = less.

sections.heading: What Shifts Supply
sections.markdown:
Remember **"ROTTEN"**:
- **R**esource and input costs: if flour gets cheaper, bakeries can make more bread at every price. Supply shifts right. If wages or fuel costs jump, supply shifts left.
- **O**ther goods' prices: a farmer can grow potatoes or wheat. If wheat prices soar, she plants more wheat and fewer potatoes, so potato supply shifts left.
- **T**axes and **subsidies**: a tax per unit raises costs and shifts supply left. A **subsidy** (government payment to producers) shifts supply right.
- **T**echnology: better machines and methods lower costs. Supply shifts right.
- **E**xpectations: if sellers expect higher prices later, they may hold back supply now.
- **N**umber of sellers: more sellers, more supply. When a dozen new coffee shops open in town, the supply of lattes goes up.
Don't forget nature and **government regulation**. A drought, early frost, or wildfire can wipe out crops and shift supply left. New safety rules can raise costs and do the same.

sections.heading: Supply Elasticity
sections.markdown:
**Elasticity of supply** measures how quickly sellers can react to a price change.
- **Elastic supply:** producers can increase output fast. T-shirts and phone cases can be cranked out in days.
- **Inelastic supply:** output can't change quickly. You can't grow more Idaho potatoes this week, build more houses this month, or create more beachfront land. Time is the biggest factor. Given years instead of weeks, almost all supply becomes more elastic.

thinkLikeAScientist.prompt:
You run a food truck at Idaho Falls' Fourth of July fireworks.
1. List two **fixed costs** and two **variable costs** for your truck.
2. Name one **ROTTEN** event that would shift your supply **left** and one that would shift it **right**. Explain how each changes what you can sell at every price.

checklist: Supply = willing AND able to sell at each price.
Law of supply: price up, quantity supplied up.
Fixed costs stay the same; variable costs grow with output.
ROTTEN: resource costs, other goods, taxes/subsidies, technology, expectations, number of sellers.
Supply is inelastic in the short run and more elastic given time.

title: Prices: Where Supply Meets Demand

sections.heading: The Concert Ticket Mystery
sections.markdown:
A huge artist announces a show in Boise. Tickets go on sale at $120. They sell out in four minutes. An hour later, resale sites list the same seats for $600.
Meanwhile, a local band plays the Idaho Center the next weekend with tickets at $40, and half the seats sit empty.
Why? Because a price works best when it lands where buyers and sellers agree. Too low and you get chaos. Too high and you get empty seats.

sections.heading: Equilibrium: The Sweet Spot
sections.markdown:
Put a demand curve and a supply curve on the same graph. Demand slopes down. Supply slopes up. They cross at one point.
That point is **equilibrium**. The price there is the **equilibrium price** (also called the market-clearing price), and the amount is the **equilibrium quantity**. At that price, the amount buyers want to buy is exactly the amount sellers want to sell. Everyone who wants one at that price gets one, and nothing is left over.
Markets naturally drift toward equilibrium. Here's how:
- **Surplus:** if the price is too high, sellers offer more than buyers want. Unsold stuff piles up, like winter coats in March. Sellers cut prices to get rid of it. The price falls toward equilibrium.
- **Shortage:** if the price is too low, buyers want more than sellers offer. Lines form, shelves go empty, and people pay resellers. Sellers realize they can charge more. The price rises toward equilibrium.
Nobody runs this. It just happens through millions of choices. That's Adam Smith's invisible hand again.

sections.heading: When the Curves Shift
sections.markdown:
Events shift supply or demand, and the equilibrium moves.
- **Demand rises** (curve shifts right): price goes **up**, quantity goes **up**. Example: a cold snap sends everyone shopping for space heaters.
- **Demand falls** (left): price **down**, quantity **down**. A recall makes people avoid a brand of lettuce.
- **Supply rises** (right): price **down**, quantity **up**. A huge potato harvest drops potato prices.
- **Supply falls** (left): price **up**, quantity **down**. A wildfire closes sawmills, and lumber prices jump.
If both curves shift at once, one of the two results (price or quantity) will be clear and the other depends on which shift is bigger.

sections.heading: Prices Are Signals
sections.markdown:
Prices do three jobs at once:
1. **They send information.** A rising price shouts, "People want more of this!"
2. **They create incentives.** High prices pull in new sellers looking for profit and push buyers to cut back or find substitutes.
3. **They ration scarce goods.** When there isn't enough for everyone, price decides who gets it: the people who value it most and can pay.
This is how a competitive market decides **what** gets made and **who** gets it, without a central planner. In 2020 and 2021, when people started building home gyms, the price of dumbbells shot up. That signal told manufacturers to make more, and within a year shelves filled up again and prices fell back.

sections.heading: When Government Sets Prices
sections.markdown:
Sometimes people think the market price is unfair, so the government sets a limit.
A **price ceiling** is a legal **maximum** price. **Rent control** is the classic example: a city says landlords can't charge more than a certain amount. It sounds helpful, but if the ceiling is below equilibrium, it causes a **shortage**: more people want apartments than landlords supply. Landlords may stop maintaining buildings or turn them into condos. People who already have a rent-controlled apartment win. People searching for one lose.
A **price floor** is a legal **minimum** price. The **minimum wage** is the best-known example. (The federal minimum is $7.25 an hour, and Idaho uses the same amount; some states set theirs much higher.) If a floor is set above equilibrium, it can cause a **surplus**. In the job market, a surplus of workers means unemployment. Economists debate how big that effect really is: some studies find modest minimum wage increases cost few jobs, while others find bigger losses, especially for teens. It depends a lot on how high the minimum is compared with local wages.
When ceilings cause shortages, a **black market** (illegal trading at higher prices) or long waiting lists often show up.

sections.heading: Rationing Without Prices
sections.markdown: If not price, then what? Societies sometimes ration by **first come, first served** (lines), **lottery** (Idaho's controlled hunt tags), **need** (organ transplants), or **coupons/quotas** (gas rationing in World War II). Each one has its own costs: time wasted in line, luck instead of value, or someone deciding who "deserves" it.

thinkLikeAScientist.prompt:
Concert tickets for a sold-out show are $120, but fans resell them for $600.
1. Was $120 above, below, or at **equilibrium**? Use the words **shortage** or **surplus** in your answer.
2. The artist could raise the price, use a lottery, or sell only at the door (first come, first served). Pick one and give one **benefit** and one **cost** of your method.

checklist: Equilibrium is where supply and demand cross: quantity demanded = quantity supplied.
Price too high = surplus; price too low = shortage. Markets push back to equilibrium.
Demand up raises price and quantity; supply up lowers price and raises quantity.
Prices send information, create incentives, and ration scarce goods.
Price ceilings (rent control) can cause shortages; price floors (minimum wage) can cause surpluses.

title: Competition and Market Structures

sections.heading: Same Product, Different Worlds
sections.markdown:
Buy a sack of potatoes at the farmers market and you've got dozens of farmers selling almost identical spuds. Nobody can charge much more than anyone else.
Now try to buy electricity for your house. In most of Idaho, one company serves your area. You can't shop around.
Both are "markets," but they work very differently. Economists sort markets into four **market structures**, based on how many sellers there are, how alike their products are, and how hard it is for new sellers to get in.

sections.heading: 1. Perfect Competition
sections.markdown:
**Perfect competition** is the textbook ideal:
- many buyers and sellers,
- identical products (economists say **standardized**),
- easy entry and exit,
- everyone has good information about prices.
No single seller can change the price. If one wheat farmer charges more, buyers go to the next farmer. Each seller is a **price taker**: they accept the market price.
Farm products like wheat, corn, and potatoes come close. Perfect competition gives buyers the lowest prices and pushes businesses to be as efficient as possible. Real markets are rarely this perfect, but it's the benchmark everything else is measured against.

sections.heading: 2. Monopolistic Competition
sections.markdown:
This one sounds scary but it's everywhere: restaurants, hair salons, clothing brands, coffee shops.
**Monopolistic competition** has:
- many sellers,
- products that are similar but **not identical**,
- fairly easy entry.
Each business tries to stand out through **product differentiation**: a different taste, location, style, service, or brand. Your favorite burger place isn't the only burger place, but it's *different* enough that you'll pay a little more. That gives each seller a tiny bit of control over price.
That's why these businesses spend so much on **advertising** and branding. They're trying to convince you that their burger is special. When they succeed, they earn some extra profit, but new competitors keep showing up to grab a share.

sections.heading: 3. Oligopoly
sections.markdown:
An **oligopoly** is a market controlled by a **few large sellers**. Think airlines, cell phone carriers, car makers, and soda. Getting in is hard because it takes huge amounts of money to start (economists call these **barriers to entry**).
In an oligopoly, each company watches the others closely. If one airline cuts fares on Boise-to-Seattle flights, the others usually match it fast. Companies may also be tempted to secretly agree on prices. That's called **collusion** or **price fixing**, and it's illegal in the U.S. A group of companies that coordinates prices and output is a **cartel**. OPEC, a group of oil-exporting countries, works this way on an international scale.

sections.heading: 4. Monopoly
sections.markdown:
A **monopoly** has **one seller** of a product with **no close substitutes**, and high barriers keep others out. The monopolist is a **price maker**: it can raise prices because buyers have nowhere else to go. Monopolies tend to charge more, produce less, and innovate less than competitive firms.
Monopolies form in a few ways:
- **Natural monopoly:** it's cheaper for one company to serve everyone, like water pipes or power lines. Building two sets of power lines down every street would be wasteful. Governments allow these but regulate their prices. Idaho Power is regulated by the Idaho Public Utilities Commission.
- **Government monopoly:** the government grants it, like the U.S. Postal Service's control of first-class mail delivery.
- **Technological monopoly:** a **patent** gives an inventor the sole right to make and sell an invention for about 20 years. A **copyright** protects books, songs, and movies. These rewards encourage people to invent and create.
- **Geographic monopoly:** the only gas station for 60 miles on a backcountry highway.

sections.heading: Keeping Competition Alive
sections.markdown:
Because competition protects consumers, the U.S. government tries to stop companies from crushing it.
- **Antitrust laws** (like the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890) make it illegal to form monopolies unfairly or fix prices. The government can block **mergers** (two companies combining into one) that would hurt competition, or even break companies up. In 1984, the government broke up the phone company AT&T into smaller companies.
- **Regulation** controls natural monopolies' prices so they can't overcharge.
- The government also protects consumers against **false advertising** and unsafe products.
Competition is a big reason market economies work. When businesses have to fight for your money, you get lower prices, better quality, and new ideas.

1. Which of the four **market structures** is it in? Give two pieces of evidence (number of sellers, how alike the products are, barriers to entry).
2. How would your price or service change if two new competitors entered that market tomorrow?

checklist: Four structures: perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, monopoly.
Perfect competition: many sellers, identical products, sellers are price takers.
Monopolistic competition: many sellers, differentiated products, lots of advertising.
Oligopoly: a few big sellers watching each other; price fixing is illegal.
Monopoly: one seller; antitrust laws and regulation protect competition and consumers.

title: Entrepreneurs and Business Organizations

sections.heading: From a Garage to the Grocery Aisle
sections.markdown:
Idaho is full of businesses that started small. Chobani's founder bought an old yogurt plant in New York with a loan and later built one of the world's biggest yogurt factories in Twin Falls. Melaleuca started in Idaho Falls and grew into a company with thousands of employees. Micron began in 1978 in the basement of a Boise dental office and became one of the biggest memory-chip makers on the planet.
Every one of those started with an **entrepreneur** who saw a chance, took a risk, and organized resources to make something people wanted.

sections.heading: What Makes an Entrepreneur
sections.markdown:
Remember from Chapter 2: **entrepreneurship** is the factor of production that pulls land, labor, and capital together. Entrepreneurs:
- spot a need or problem people will pay to solve,
- take on **risk**, putting their own time and money on the line,
- **innovate**, finding a new product or a better way to do something,
- organize workers and resources.
Their reward is **profit**: the money left after paying all costs. **Profit = revenue - costs.** **Revenue** is all the money that comes in from sales.
Most new businesses struggle early. Federal data show roughly 1 in 5 new businesses closes within its first year, and about half are gone within five years. The ones that survive usually had a clear plan, enough money to get through slow months, and something customers truly wanted.
A **business plan** is the map: what you'll sell, who will buy it, who your competitors are, what it'll cost, how you'll get the money, and how you'll make a profit.

sections.heading: Three Main Types of Business
sections.markdown:
When you start a business, you choose how to organize it. Each type has trade-offs.
**Sole proprietorship**: one owner.
- **Pros:** easy and cheap to start, you're the boss, you keep all the profit.
- **Cons:** **unlimited liability**, meaning if the business owes money or gets sued, the owner's personal savings, car, and house can be taken. It's also hard to raise money, and the business may end if the owner quits or dies.
- Most U.S. businesses are sole proprietorships: lawn mowing, photographers, food trucks.
**Partnership**: two or more owners sharing the business.
- **Pros:** more money and more skills (one partner knows cooking, the other knows marketing).
- **Cons:** partners usually share unlimited liability, and disagreements can wreck the business. Partners should write a **partnership agreement** that spells out who does what and who gets what.
**Corporation**: a business that is a legal "person" separate from its owners.
- Owners buy **stock**, which are small pieces of ownership. Owners of stock are called **stockholders** or **shareholders**.
- **Pros:** **limited liability** (owners can only lose what they invested, not their houses), easy to raise lots of money by selling stock, and the company keeps going even when owners change.
- **Cons:** expensive and complicated to set up, lots of rules, and **double taxation**: the corporation pays tax on its profit, and stockholders pay tax again on the **dividends** (profit payouts) they receive.
- Corporations are a small share of businesses but earn most of the total sales in the U.S.

sections.heading: Other Ways to Organize
sections.markdown:
- **LLC (limited liability company):** a popular mix. Owners get limited liability like a corporation, but taxes work more like a partnership. Many small Idaho businesses are LLCs.
- **Franchise:** you buy the right to use a big company's name and system. Many fast-food restaurants work this way. You get a proven brand and training, but you pay fees and follow their rules.
- **Cooperative (co-op):** owned by its members, who share the benefits. Many farmers sell crops through co-ops, and credit unions are co-ops for banking.
- **Nonprofit:** an organization that doesn't aim to earn profit for owners, like a food bank, a hospital, or a youth sports league.

sections.heading: How Businesses Grow
sections.markdown: Businesses grow by reinvesting profit, borrowing, selling stock, or combining with others through **mergers**. Some grow so big they operate in many countries. Those are **multinational corporations**. You'll see in Chapter 22 that specialization and trade help businesses reach customers far beyond Idaho.

You want to start a business this summer (pick one: lawn care, phone repair, baked goods, photography, or your own idea).
1. Which business organization would you choose and why? Name one **advantage** and one **risk**.
2. Estimate your first month: list two costs, guess your revenue, and calculate your **profit** (profit = revenue - costs).

checklist: Entrepreneurs spot needs, take risks, innovate, and earn profit (revenue - costs).
Sole proprietorship: easy, all profit is yours, but unlimited liability.
Partnership: shared money and skills, shared liability, possible conflict.
Corporation: limited liability and easy to raise money, but complex and double-taxed.
Other options: LLCs, franchises, co-ops, and nonprofits.

title: Labor, Wages, and Your Career

sections.heading: Why Does That Job Pay So Much?
sections.markdown:
A lifeguard at the city pool might earn $12 to $15 an hour. A lineworker who climbs power poles in a blizzard can earn $45 or more. A surgeon earns way more than that.
Is it because surgeons are better people than lifeguards? Nope. It's supply and demand, the same tools from Unit 2, applied to the **labor market**.

sections.heading: The Labor Market
sections.markdown:
In the labor market, the "product" is work.
- **Workers supply labor.** They're the sellers.
- **Employers demand labor.** They're the buyers.
- The "price" is the **wage**.
The **labor force** is everyone 16 or older who has a job or is actively looking for one. Students who aren't job hunting, retirees, and people who've stopped looking aren't counted.
**Demand for labor** is called a **derived demand**: businesses only want workers because customers want the stuff those workers make. When people buy more houses, demand for carpenters goes up.

sections.heading: What Decides Your Wage
sections.markdown:
Wages land at the equilibrium where labor supply meets labor demand. Things that push wages up:
- **Skills and education (human capital).** Jobs that take years of training have fewer qualified workers. Low supply, high pay.
- **High demand.** Fields that are booming, like nursing, electricians, and software, bid wages up.
- **Danger or tough conditions.** Hazardous or unpleasant jobs often pay more to attract workers.
- **Location.** Wages and living costs vary a lot. Boise pays differently than rural Idaho or Seattle.
- **Productivity.** Workers who produce more value usually earn more.
Jobs are often grouped by skill level: **unskilled** (little training), **semiskilled** (some training), **skilled** (lots of training, like a plumber or welder), and **professional** (advanced degree, like a pharmacist or engineer).
Education matters. Bureau of Labor Statistics data show that, on average, people with more education earn more and are unemployed less often. A college degree pays off for many careers, but so do apprenticeships and trade certificates. Lots of skilled trades pay well and come without huge student debt.

sections.heading: Labor Unions
sections.markdown:
A **labor union** is a group of workers who join together to bargain with employers over pay, benefits, and working conditions. Instead of each worker negotiating alone, the union negotiates for everyone through **collective bargaining**.
Unions grew during the Industrial Revolution, when many workers faced 12-hour days, child labor, and dangerous factories. Unions helped win the 8-hour day and weekends. If talks fail, a union may **strike**, meaning workers refuse to work until a deal is reached.
Union membership in the U.S. has fallen a lot since the 1950s and is now around 10 percent of workers. Idaho is a **right-to-work** state, which means workers can't be required to join a union or pay union fees to keep a job. People debate unions: supporters say they protect workers and the middle class, while critics say they can raise costs and make it harder for businesses to adapt.

sections.heading: Your Paycheck: Gross vs. Net
sections.markdown:
Your first paycheck might be a shock. If you earn $15 an hour for 20 hours, that's $300. That's your **gross pay**. But your check will be less. That's your **net pay** (take-home pay).
The difference comes from **deductions**:
- **Federal income tax** (depends on your income and the W-4 form you fill out when you're hired).
- **State income tax** (Idaho has a flat rate, 5.3 percent as of 2026).
- **FICA taxes**: 6.2 percent for **Social Security** and 1.45 percent for **Medicare**.
- Sometimes health insurance or retirement savings.
Your **pay stub** lists all of this. Read it every time. Mistakes happen.
Besides wages, many jobs offer **benefits**: health insurance, paid time off, and retirement plans like a **401(k)**, where some employers add matching money. A job paying slightly less with great benefits can be worth more than one paying more with none.

sections.heading: Building Your Career
sections.markdown:
Your career is a long hike, not a single step. A few moves that pay off for decades:
- Build **human capital** through school, training, certifications, and apprenticeships.
- Explore options. Idaho's fastest-growing fields include health care, construction, and tech.
- Practice **soft skills**: showing up on time, communicating, teamwork, and solving problems. Employers consistently rank these near the top of what they want.
- Remember the opportunity cost of training: time and money now for higher pay later. For most people, it's one of the best investments they'll ever make.

2. If you earn $16/hour for 25 hours a week, what's your **gross pay** for the week? Estimate your **net pay** after FICA (7.65 percent) and Idaho tax (5.3 percent). Show your math.

checklist: Labor market: workers supply labor, employers demand it, the wage is the price.
More skills, high demand, danger, and productivity push wages up.
Unions bargain collectively; Idaho is a right-to-work state.
Gross pay minus deductions (taxes, FICA) = net pay.
Human capital and soft skills are long-term career investments.

title: Money and Banking

sections.heading: Trading Without Money
sections.markdown:
Imagine there's no money. You have a basket of huckleberries and you want a new fishing reel. You find a guy with a reel, but he doesn't want huckleberries. He wants firewood. Now you need to find someone with firewood who wants huckleberries. Good luck.
This is **barter**: trading goods directly for other goods. It only works when both people want exactly what the other has. Economists call that the **double coincidence of wants**, and it almost never happens. That's why every society eventually invents money.

sections.heading: The Three Jobs of Money
sections.markdown:
**Money** is anything people widely accept as payment. It does three jobs:
1. **Medium of exchange:** you use it to buy things. Nobody has to want your huckleberries.
2. **Store of value:** you can save it and spend it later. Huckleberries rot. Dollars don't (though inflation can eat at them, as you'll see in Chapter 17).
3. **Unit of account:** it's a common measuring stick. Everything has a price in dollars, so you can compare a $40 fishing reel with a $12 pizza.
Good money has six **characteristics**: it's **durable** (lasts), **portable** (easy to carry), **divisible** (can be broken into smaller amounts), **uniform** (every dollar is the same), **limited in supply** (scarce), and **acceptable** (people will take it).

sections.heading: Kinds of Money
sections.markdown:
Throughout history, people have used shells, salt, cattle, and beaver pelts. Fur traders in early Idaho used beaver pelts as money.
- **Commodity money** has value by itself, like gold, silver, or salt.
- **Representative money** is paper you can trade in for something valuable, like early U.S. dollars that could be swapped for gold or silver.
- **Fiat money** has value only because the government says it's legal money and people trust it. Today's U.S. dollar is fiat money. The U.S. ended the gold standard completely in 1971. A dollar is worth something because everyone agrees it is and the government accepts it for taxes.
Today, most money isn't paper at all. It's numbers in bank accounts, moved by debit cards, phone apps, and direct deposit.

sections.heading: The Money Supply
sections.markdown:
Economists measure how much money is out there. The **money supply** has two main measures:
- **M1:** money you can spend right now: cash, checking accounts, and (since 2020) regular savings deposits.
- **M2:** everything in M1 plus "near money" that's easy to turn into cash, like small CDs and money market funds.
The Federal Reserve watches and influences the money supply. You'll meet the Fed in Chapter 21.

sections.heading: How Banks Work
sections.markdown:
A **bank** is a business that keeps people's money safe, lends it out, and earns a profit doing it.
Here's the basic deal: you **deposit** $1,000. The bank keeps a slice on hand and **lends** most of the rest to someone buying a truck. The borrower pays the bank **interest**, the price of borrowing money. The bank pays you a smaller interest rate on your savings and keeps the difference as profit.
That lending actually **creates money**. Your $1,000 is still in your account, *and* the borrower now has hundreds of dollars to spend. When the borrower spends it, it lands in someone else's bank, which lends some of it out again. This is called **fractional reserve banking**: banks keep only a fraction of deposits as **reserves**.
Types of financial institutions:
- **Commercial banks** (like big national banks or local Idaho banks): checking, savings, and loans for people and businesses.
- **Credit unions** (like Idaho Central Credit Union): nonprofit co-ops owned by their members. They often have lower fees and better rates.
- **Savings and loans**: historically focused on home loans.
- **Online banks**: no branches, often higher savings rates.

sections.heading: Is My Money Safe?
sections.markdown:
In the Great Depression of the 1930s, thousands of banks failed. When people feared a bank was in trouble, they all rushed to pull out their money at once. That's a **bank run**, and since banks lend most deposits out, they couldn't pay everyone. People lost their life savings.
In 1933, Congress created the **FDIC** (Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation). If an FDIC-insured bank fails, the government guarantees your deposits up to **$250,000** per person, per bank, per account type. Credit unions have the same protection through the **NCUA**. Since the FDIC started, no one has lost a penny of insured deposits.
Banks are also checked by government regulators to make sure they're not taking crazy risks. When banks do take crazy risks, like in the 2008 financial crisis, the whole economy can get dragged down. You'll see that story in Chapter 18.

1. Rate each option on at least **three** of the six characteristics of money (durable, portable, divisible, uniform, limited supply, acceptable).
2. Which would you choose, and what would the council need to do to make people **trust** it?

checklist: Barter is hard because of the double coincidence of wants.
Money is a medium of exchange, a store of value, and a unit of account.
Today's dollar is fiat money: valuable because people trust it and the government backs it.
Banks lend out most deposits, earn interest, and create money through fractional reserve banking.
The FDIC insures bank deposits up to $250,000; the NCUA does the same for credit unions.

title: Checking, Savings, and Modern Money Tools

sections.heading: Your First Account
sections.markdown:
Your first real paycheck shows up. Your employer offers **direct deposit**, which sends your pay straight into a bank account. No account? You'll be cashing checks at a store that charges a fee every single time.
Opening an account is one of the first grown-up money moves you'll make. Here's how to do it well.

sections.heading: Checking Accounts: Money in Motion
sections.markdown:
A **checking account** is for everyday spending. Money goes in (paychecks, deposits) and comes out (debit card swipes, bills, transfers). It earns little or no interest because it's built for access, not growth.
With a checking account you usually get:
- a **debit card**, which pulls money straight out of your account when you pay,
- online and mobile banking, so you can check your **balance** anytime,
- the ability to pay bills automatically and send money with apps.
To open one, you usually need ID, your Social Security number, and a small first deposit. Under 18? Most banks need a parent or guardian on the account.
**Watch out for fees:**
- **Overdraft fee:** if you spend more than you have, the bank may cover it and charge you $25 to $35. Three small coffees can turn into a $100 mistake. You can usually **opt out** of overdraft coverage so the card just gets declined instead.
- **Monthly maintenance fee:** some accounts charge a monthly fee unless you keep a minimum balance or have direct deposit.
- **ATM fees:** using an out-of-network ATM can cost $3 to $5 a pop.
Look for accounts with no monthly fee and lots of free ATMs. Credit unions and online banks are often good at this.

sections.heading: Keeping Track of Your Money
sections.markdown:
Every account has a **statement** (monthly summary) and a running list of **transactions**. Check them. **Reconciling** your account means comparing your own records with the bank's to make sure they match and to catch errors or fraud fast.
Simple habits: check your banking app a couple of times a week, turn on low-balance alerts, and know your **available balance** before you swipe. Pending charges may not show up right away.
If you ever write a paper **check**, you'll fill in the date, the person's name, the amount in numbers and words, and your signature. Checks are rarer now, but landlords and some employers still use them.

sections.heading: Savings Accounts: Money at Rest
sections.markdown:
A **savings account** is where money sits and grows. Banks pay you **interest** for keeping it there. The rate is shown as the **APY** (annual percentage yield), which includes **compound interest**, interest earned on your interest. (Chapter 12 shows just how powerful that gets.)
Rates vary a lot. Big traditional banks sometimes pay almost nothing, while **high-yield savings accounts**, often at online banks, may pay many times more. It's worth comparing.
Other savings tools:
- **Certificate of deposit (CD):** you agree to leave money in for a set time (6 months, 1 year, 5 years) for a higher rate. Pull it out early and you pay a penalty.
- **Money market account:** savings with a higher rate and sometimes limited check writing, often with a higher minimum balance.
The more access you give up, the higher the rate you usually get. That's a trade-off.
Your first big savings goal should be an **emergency fund**: money set aside for surprises like a car repair, a medical bill, or losing a job. A common target for adults is 3 to 6 months of expenses. For a teen, even $500 is a strong start.

sections.heading: Modern Money Tools
sections.markdown:
Money moves in new ways now, and the basic rules still apply.
- **Mobile payment apps** (like Venmo, Cash App, Zelle, Apple Pay) make paying friends easy. But payments to a stranger are often like handing over cash: hard or impossible to get back. Only send money to people you know.
- **Buy now, pay later (BNPL)** splits purchases into installments. It feels painless but makes it easy to overspend, and missed payments can bring fees and hurt your credit.
- **Cryptocurrencies** like Bitcoin are digital tokens not issued by any government. Prices swing wildly, they are not FDIC insured, and scams are common. Treat them as high-risk.
- **Prepaid debit cards** work without a bank account but often carry fees.

sections.heading: Protect Yourself
sections.markdown:
**Identity theft** is when someone steals your personal information to open accounts or spend money in your name. Scammers fish for it with fake texts, emails, and calls (**phishing**). Smart defenses:
- Never share your PIN, passwords, or one-time codes. Your bank will never ask for them.
- Use strong, different passwords and turn on two-factor authentication.
- Don't click links in surprise texts about your "account." Go to the bank's app yourself.
- Report a lost card or strange charge right away. Federal law limits what you owe for fraud on debit cards, but only if you report it fast.

1. Compare two real or imagined accounts: one with a $10 monthly fee and $35 overdraft fee, and one credit union account with no monthly fee. Which do you choose and why?
2. Make a simple plan: how much of each paycheck goes to spending, to savings, and toward an emergency fund goal? Name the type of account each one lives in.

checklist: Checking accounts are for spending; savings accounts are for growing money.
Avoid overdraft, monthly, and out-of-network ATM fees.
APY shows the real yearly return, including compound interest.
Build an emergency fund first: about 3 to 6 months of expenses for adults.
Payment apps, BNPL, and crypto are useful but risky; guard your passwords, PINs, and codes.

title: Investing: Stocks, Bonds, and Compound Interest

sections.heading: The Snowball on the Mountain
sections.markdown:
Push a small snowball off the top of a steep slope. At first it barely grows. But each roll picks up more snow, and the bigger it gets, the more snow it grabs. By the bottom it's huge.
That's **compound interest**, and it's the most powerful money idea you'll learn this year.

sections.heading: Saving vs. Investing
sections.markdown:
**Saving** means setting money aside somewhere safe, like a savings account, for short-term goals and emergencies. It's low risk, but it grows slowly.
**Investing** means using money to buy assets that you hope will grow in value over time, like stocks, bonds, and real estate. It can grow much faster, but there's **risk**: you could lose money.
The basic rule: **the higher the possible return, the higher the risk.** A savings account is safe but earns little. Stocks can grow a lot but can also drop 30 percent in a bad year.

sections.heading: Compound Interest: Time Is Your Superpower
sections.markdown:
**Simple interest** pays only on your original money (the **principal**). **Compound interest** pays on your principal *and* on all the interest you've already earned.
Say you invest $1,000 earning 8 percent a year:
- After 1 year: $1,080
- After 10 years: about $2,159
- After 30 years: about $10,063
- After 40 years: about $21,725
You never added another dollar. Time did the work.
That's why starting early matters so much. Two hikers:
- **Ava** invests $100 a month from age 18 to 28, then stops. Total put in: about $12,000.
- **Ben** waits and invests $100 a month from 28 to 65. Total put in: about $44,000.
At 8 percent, Ava ends up with *more* money at 65 than Ben, even though she put in less than a third as much. She gave compound interest a 10-year head start.
A shortcut called the **Rule of 72** tells you how long it takes money to double: divide 72 by the interest rate. At 8 percent, money doubles about every 9 years. At 2 percent, it takes about 36 years.

sections.heading: Stocks
sections.markdown:
A **stock** is a small piece of ownership in a corporation. Own one share of a company and you own a tiny slice of it.
You can make money from stocks two ways:
1. **Capital gain**: the price goes up and you sell for more than you paid.
2. **Dividends**: some companies pay part of their profits to stockholders.
Stocks are bought and sold on **stock exchanges** like the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq. A **stock market index** like the S&P 500 tracks a group of big companies to show how the market overall is doing. A long rise is called a **bull market**; a drop of 20 percent or more is a **bear market**.
Over the long run, U.S. stocks have historically averaged roughly 10 percent a year before inflation, but with big ups and downs. Some years drop a lot. That's why stocks are for money you won't need for many years.

sections.heading: Bonds
sections.markdown:
A **bond** is a loan you make to a government or company. They promise to pay you interest and give back the **face value** on a set **maturity date**.
- **U.S. Treasury bonds** are backed by the federal government and are considered very safe.
- **Municipal bonds** come from cities and states, often to build schools and roads.
- **Corporate bonds** pay more interest but carry more risk; a company can go bankrupt.
Bonds usually earn less than stocks but swing less, too.

sections.heading: Funds: Buying the Whole Trail Mix
sections.markdown:
Picking one company is risky. If it fails, you lose. **Diversification** means spreading your money across many investments so one loss doesn't sink you. Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
The easy way to diversify:
- A **mutual fund** pools money from many investors to buy many stocks or bonds, managed by professionals.
- An **index fund** simply buys every company in an index, like the S&P 500. It's cheap and well diversified.
- An **ETF (exchange-traded fund)** is like an index fund that trades like a stock.
Watch the **fees**, sometimes shown as an **expense ratio**. A fund charging 1 percent a year versus 0.05 percent can cost you tens of thousands of dollars over a lifetime.

sections.heading: Retirement Accounts and Your Plan
sections.markdown:
The government gives tax breaks to encourage saving for retirement:
- A **401(k)** through your employer. If your boss offers a **match**, take it. It's free money.
- An **IRA** (individual retirement account) you open yourself. A **Roth IRA** is especially good for young workers: you pay taxes now, then the money grows tax-free. You can open one as soon as you have earned income from a job.
Good investing matches your **financial plan**: Is this for something next year (keep it safe) or 40 years away (you can handle more risk)? Know your **goal**, your **time horizon**, and your **risk tolerance**.
And beware anything that promises big returns with "no risk." That's the classic sign of a scam, like a **Ponzi scheme**, which pays early investors with money from new ones until it collapses.

thinkLikeAScientist.prompt:
You have $2,000 from summer work. You'll need $500 for a car repair fund, and the rest is for something 20+ years away.
1. Where would you put each part (savings, CD, bond, index fund, single stock)? Explain using **risk**, **return**, and **time horizon**.
2. Use the **Rule of 72** to estimate how many times your long-term money would double in 36 years at 8 percent. About how much might it grow to?

checklist: Saving is safe and slow; investing can grow faster but carries risk.
Compound interest earns interest on interest; starting early is the biggest advantage.
Rule of 72: 72 ÷ interest rate ≈ years to double.
Stocks = ownership; bonds = loans; funds spread your money out (diversification).
Use retirement accounts (401(k) match, Roth IRA) and match investments to your goal and time horizon.

title: Budgeting and Smart Spending

sections.heading: Where Did It All Go?
sections.markdown:
You get paid Friday. By Wednesday you're checking couches for change. You didn't buy anything big. Just gas, a few lunches, a game, some snacks, a subscription you forgot about. Money leaks out in small drips.
A **budget** is a plan that tells your money where to go *before* it leaks. It's not a punishment. It's a trail map.

sections.heading: Start With Goals
sections.markdown:
Good budgets start with **financial goals**. Make them **SMART**: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound.
- Not SMART: "Save money."
- SMART: "Save $1,800 for a used car by next July by putting $150 a month into savings."
Goals come in three lengths: **short-term** (less than a year: concert tickets), **medium-term** (1 to 5 years: a car, college costs), and **long-term** (5+ years: a house, retirement).

sections.heading: Building a Monthly Budget
sections.markdown:
A budget compares **income** with **expenses**.
**Income:** your **net pay** (take-home, after taxes from Chapter 9), plus any other money that comes in.
**Expenses** come in two kinds:
- **Fixed expenses** are the same every month: rent, car payment, insurance, phone plan.
- **Variable expenses** change month to month: groceries, gas, eating out, entertainment, clothes.
And don't forget **savings**. Treat it like a bill. **Pay yourself first**: move savings out the moment you get paid, before you can spend it.
A popular starting guide is the **50/30/20 rule**:
- **50%** for needs (housing, food, transportation, insurance, minimum debt payments),
- **30%** for wants (fun, eating out, hobbies),
- **20%** for savings and paying extra on debt.
Example for someone taking home $3,000 a month: $1,500 needs, $900 wants, $600 savings. It's a starting point. In an expensive city, needs might take more.
If expenses are bigger than income, you have a **deficit**. Fix it by cutting expenses or earning more. If income is bigger, you have a **surplus**. Send it toward your goals.
A **zero-based budget** gives every dollar a job, so income minus everything you planned equals zero. That doesn't mean you spend it all. It means every dollar has a purpose, including savings.

sections.heading: Track It
sections.markdown:
A budget only works if you check it. Track spending for a month using a banking app, a spreadsheet, or receipts. Most people are shocked by one category. (It's usually food.)
Watch out for:
- **Subscriptions** you forgot: streaming, apps, gaming passes.
- **Lifestyle creep**: spending more just because you earn more.
- **Impulse buys**: wait 24 hours before any unplanned purchase over $50. Most of the urge fades.

sections.heading: Smart Shopping
sections.markdown:
**Comparison shopping** means checking prices and quality at more than one place before you buy.
- Compare **unit prices** (cost per ounce or per item). The big box isn't always cheaper.
- Read reviews from multiple sources, not just the seller's site.
- Know the **total cost**: shipping, tax, fees, and add-ons. Idaho charges a 6 percent sales tax on most purchases, including groceries. (Idaho gives residents a **food tax credit**, $155 per person in 2026, to offset part of that.)
- Be skeptical of advertising tricks: "limited time," "only 2 left," and prices ending in .99.
- Generic and store brands are often made in the same factories as name brands for less.

sections.heading: Big Purchases: Cars and College
sections.markdown:
For big purchases, a small percentage difference is real money.
**Cars:** Research reliability. Compare the **total cost of ownership**: price, interest on a loan, insurance, gas, and repairs. A used car a few years old often saves thousands because new cars lose value (**depreciation**) fast in the first years. Get a mechanic to inspect a used car before you buy.
**College and training** may be the biggest purchase you make before 25, so shop for it like one.
- Compare the **net price** (cost after grants and scholarships), not the sticker price. Every college has a **net price calculator** on its website.
- Fill out the **FAFSA** (Free Application for Federal Student Aid) every year to qualify for grants, work-study, and federal loans.
- **Grants and scholarships** don't have to be paid back. Loans do, with interest.
- Look at Idaho options: the **Idaho Opportunity Scholarship**, Idaho's community colleges and technical colleges, and dual credit classes you can take in high school.
- Compare costs to likely earnings in your field. Borrowing $80,000 for a career that starts at $35,000 a year is a heavy pack to carry up the mountain.
