You take home $1,600 a month from a full-time summer job and live at home.
1. Build a monthly budget using the **50/30/20 rule**. List at least two fixed and three variable expenses with dollar amounts.
2. Set one **SMART** goal and show how your budget gets you there.

checklist: A budget plans where income goes: needs, wants, savings.
Fixed expenses stay the same; variable expenses change.
Pay yourself first; the 50/30/20 rule is a good starting guide.
Comparison shop: unit prices, total cost, reviews, and sales tax.
For cars and college, compare total cost and net price, and fill out the FAFSA.

title: Credit, Debt, and Your Credit Score

sections.heading: Borrowing a Rope
sections.markdown:
On a hard climb, a rope can save you. Tie in wrong or lean on it too much and it can pull you right off the mountain.
**Credit** works the same way. Used well, it gets you a car to commute to work, a college degree, or a house. Used carelessly, it can take years to climb out from under.

sections.heading: What Credit Is
sections.markdown:
**Credit** means borrowing money now and promising to pay it back later, usually with **interest**. The person or business lending is the **creditor** (or lender). You, the borrower, are the **debtor**. The money you owe is **debt**.
The cost of borrowing is shown as the **APR** (annual percentage rate). It includes interest and some fees, so it's the best number for comparing loans. Lower is better.
The **principal** is the amount you borrowed. Your payments go toward interest first, then principal.

sections.heading: Types of Credit
sections.markdown:
**Installment credit**: you borrow a set amount and repay it in equal monthly payments over a set time.
- **Auto loans** (often 3 to 6 years)
- **Student loans**
- **Mortgages** (home loans, often 15 or 30 years)
Many of these are **secured loans**, meaning backed by **collateral**, something the lender can take if you don't pay. Miss car payments and the lender can **repossess** the car. Miss mortgage payments and you can face **foreclosure** and lose the house.
**Revolving credit**: you get a **credit limit** and can borrow, repay, and borrow again.
- **Credit cards** are the most common. If you pay the full **statement balance** every month, you usually pay **no interest**. If you only pay the **minimum payment**, interest piles up fast. Credit card APRs often run above 20 percent.
**Unsecured loans** have no collateral, like most credit cards and personal loans. They usually cost more because they're riskier for the lender.

sections.heading: Comparing Your Options
sections.markdown:
Before you borrow, research the choices:
- **Banks and credit unions**: often the best rates for car and personal loans. Credit unions frequently beat banks.
- **Dealer financing**: convenient, and sometimes has deals, but compare it with a credit union's offer first.
- **Federal student loans** (from the FAFSA): fixed rates and flexible repayment plans. Use these before private student loans.
- **Store cards and buy-now-pay-later**: easy to get, easy to overspend, and sometimes high fees.
- **Payday loans** and **title loans**: very fast cash, but fees often equal APRs of 300 percent or more. They trap many borrowers in debt. Avoid them.
Always ask: What's the APR? What's the total I'll pay over the life of the loan? Are there fees or penalties?

sections.heading: The Minimum Payment Trap
sections.markdown:
Say you owe $2,000 on a credit card at 24 percent APR and pay only $50 a month. It would take almost 7 years to pay off, and you'd pay about $2,000 in interest. Your $2,000 of stuff would really cost about $4,000.
Pay the whole balance every month and that number is **zero**. That's the golden rule of credit cards.

sections.heading: Your Credit Score
sections.markdown:
Lenders want to know: will this person pay me back? Your **credit history**, the record of how you've handled debt, answers that. It lives in your **credit report**, kept by three **credit bureaus**: Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion.
A **credit score** turns that history into a three-digit number. The most common, the **FICO score**, runs from **300 to 850**. Higher means more **creditworthy**. FICO's own breakdown of what matters:
- **Payment history (about 35%)**: do you pay on time? This is the biggest factor. One payment 30 days late can drop a score a lot.
- **Amounts owed (about 30%)**: how much of your available credit you use. This is your **credit utilization**. Keep it under 30 percent, and lower is better.
- **Length of credit history (about 15%)**: older accounts help.
- **New credit (about 10%)**: applying for lots of cards in a short time can lower your score.
- **Credit mix (about 10%)**: having different types (a card and a car loan) helps a little.
Why it matters: a better score means lower interest rates, which can save you thousands of dollars on a car or house. Landlords, insurance companies, and some employers may check your credit too.
You can check your credit reports for free at **AnnualCreditReport.com**. Look for mistakes or accounts you didn't open (a sign of identity theft), and dispute errors.

sections.heading: Building Credit the Right Way
sections.markdown:
You can't get a good score with no history. Ways to start:
- Become an **authorized user** on a parent's card (only if they pay on time).
- Get a **secured credit card**, which uses a cash deposit as your limit.
- Use a card for one small bill, like your phone, and pay it in full automatically every month.
And if debt does get out of hand, talk to the lender early, and look for a reputable nonprofit **credit counselor**. **Bankruptcy** is a legal last resort that can wipe out or restructure some debts, but it stays on your credit report for 7 to 10 years.

thinkLikeAScientist.prompt:
You need a $10,000 car loan for 5 years. A credit union offers 7 percent APR. The dealer offers 12 percent APR.
1. The monthly payments are about $198 (7%) and $222 (12%). How much would you pay **in total** for each loan over 60 months? How much does the better rate save you?
2. Name two habits that would raise your **credit score** before you apply, and explain which score factor each one improves.

checklist: Credit = borrow now, pay back later with interest; compare loans using APR.
Installment loans (car, student, mortgage) vs. revolving credit (credit cards).
Pay the full credit card balance every month to avoid interest; avoid payday loans.
FICO scores run 300 to 850; payment history and amounts owed matter most.
Check your free credit reports at AnnualCreditReport.com.

title: Insurance, Risk, and Consumer Protection

sections.heading: Why Pack a First-Aid Kit?
sections.markdown:
You probably won't twist an ankle on this hike. But if you do, five miles from the trailhead, you'll be really glad you packed the wrap and the ibuprofen.
**Insurance** is the money version of a first-aid kit. You pay a little now so that a big, rare disaster doesn't wreck your finances.

sections.heading: How Insurance Works
sections.markdown:
Life is full of **risk**: a car crash, a house fire, a broken leg, a death in the family. You can handle risk four ways:
1. **Avoid** it (don't ride a motorcycle).
2. **Reduce** it (wear a helmet, install smoke alarms).
3. **Keep** it (pay for small stuff yourself, like a cracked phone screen).
4. **Transfer** it to an insurance company.
Insurance works by **pooling risk**. Thousands of people pay a **premium** (a regular payment) into a big pool. Most of them won't have a disaster this year. The few who do get paid from the pool. You're trading a small, certain cost for protection from a big, uncertain one.
Key terms in every **policy** (your insurance contract):
- **Premium:** what you pay, monthly or yearly, to stay covered.
- **Deductible:** what you pay out of pocket before insurance starts paying. A $500 deductible means you cover the first $500 of a claim.
- **Claim:** your request for the insurance company to pay.
- **Coverage limit:** the most the policy will pay.
Higher deductible = lower premium (you're keeping more risk). Lower deductible = higher premium. Choose a deductible you could actually pay from your emergency fund.

sections.heading: Auto Insurance
sections.markdown:
Idaho, like almost every state, **requires** drivers to carry auto **liability insurance**. Liability pays for injuries and damage you cause to *other* people and their property. Idaho's minimum is often written as **25/50/15**: up to $25,000 for one person's injuries, $50,000 for all injuries in one crash, and $15,000 for property damage. Many experts recommend more, because a serious crash can easily cost far more than the minimum.
Other common coverage:
- **Collision:** pays to fix *your* car after a crash.
- **Comprehensive:** pays for theft, hail, fire, or hitting a deer on Highway 20.
- **Uninsured motorist:** protects you if the other driver has no insurance.
Teen drivers pay some of the highest premiums because, statistically, they crash more. Good grades discounts, a clean driving record, and a safer car can lower your rate.

sections.heading: Health Insurance
sections.markdown:
Medical bills are a leading cause of money trouble in America. One night in a hospital can cost thousands of dollars. Health insurance terms:
- **Copay:** a set fee for a visit, like $30.
- **Coinsurance:** after you meet your deductible, you pay a share (like 20 percent) and the insurer pays the rest.
- **Out-of-pocket maximum:** the most you'll pay in a year. After that, the plan pays 100 percent of covered costs.
- **In-network** doctors cost less than **out-of-network** ones.
Most people get health insurance through an employer. Young adults can usually stay on a parent's plan until age **26**. Others buy plans through the **Health Insurance Marketplace** (Your Health Idaho in our state) or qualify for government programs like **Medicaid** (low-income) or **Medicare** (65 and older).

sections.heading: Home, Renters, and Life Insurance
sections.markdown:
- **Homeowners insurance** covers the house and belongings from fire, theft, and storms, plus liability if someone gets hurt on your property. Mortgage lenders require it.
- **Renters insurance** covers your stuff (laptop, clothes, bike) in an apartment. It's usually cheap, often around $15 to $20 a month. Your landlord's insurance covers the building, not your things.
- **Life insurance** pays money to your **beneficiaries** (people you name) if you die. It matters most when others depend on your income, like kids. **Term life** covers a set number of years and is cheap. **Whole life** lasts your whole life and builds some cash value but costs much more.
- **Disability insurance** replaces part of your income if an injury or illness keeps you from working.

sections.heading: Consumer Rights and Protection
sections.markdown:
Smart consumers know their rights and the tools that protect them.
- The **Federal Trade Commission (FTC)** fights false advertising and scams.
- The **Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)** handles complaints about banks, loans, and credit cards.
- The **Idaho Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division** helps with scams and unfair business practices in Idaho.
- A **warranty** is the seller's promise to fix or replace a product. Read what it covers and for how long.
- If something goes wrong, keep receipts, contact the seller first, put complaints in writing, and escalate to these agencies if needed.
Common scams to watch for: fake job offers that ask you to pay first, "you won a prize, just pay the shipping," romance and crypto scams, and anyone demanding payment in **gift cards** (no real business or government agency asks for that).

1. Quote A: $1,500 deductible, $110/month premium. Quote B: $500 deductible, $150/month. Which do you choose? Use your emergency fund, risk, and the yearly cost difference to explain.
2. Name two ways you could lower your premium.

checklist: Insurance pools risk: many pay premiums so the few with disasters get paid.
Higher deductible means lower premium, and the reverse.
Idaho requires auto liability insurance (minimum 25/50/15).
Health terms: copay, coinsurance, out-of-pocket maximum; stay on a parent's plan until 26.
Renters, life, and disability insurance; know your consumer rights (FTC, CFPB, Idaho Attorney General).

title: GDP and Economic Growth

sections.heading: The View From the Ridge
sections.markdown:
Up to now, you've been looking at single trees: one buyer, one business, one paycheck. Climb onto the ridge and you can see the whole forest. That's **macroeconomics**: the economy as one giant system.
The first question from up here: How big is the whole economy, and is it growing?

sections.heading: Gross Domestic Product
sections.markdown:
**Gross domestic product (GDP)** is the total market value of all **final** goods and services produced **within a country** in a given year.
Let's unpack that:
- **Market value:** everything is measured in dollars, so we can add potatoes and haircuts together.
- **Final goods:** only things sold to the end user count. The flour a bakery buys is an **intermediate good**; it's already counted in the price of the bread. Counting both would be double counting.
- **Within a country:** a Toyota made in Kentucky counts in U.S. GDP. A Nike shoe made in Vietnam doesn't.
- **In a given year:** a used car sold this year was already counted when it was new. It doesn't count again.
What's *not* in GDP: used goods, stocks and bonds (those are ownership changes, not production), unpaid work like chores, and illegal or under-the-table activity (the **underground economy**).
U.S. GDP is more than $30 trillion a year, the largest in the world. Idaho's economy is one of the fastest-growing in the country in recent years.

sections.heading: Two Ways to Count
sections.markdown:
**Expenditure approach:** add up everything spent on final goods and services. Economists write it as:
**GDP = C + I + G + (X - M)**
- **C, consumption:** household spending on goods and services. This is by far the biggest piece, about two-thirds of U.S. GDP.
- **I, investment:** businesses buying capital (machines, buildings) plus new houses. (Not stocks!)
- **G, government purchases:** roads, schools, military equipment, government workers' pay.
- **X - M, net exports:** exports minus imports. The U.S. usually imports more than it exports, so this number is negative.
**Income approach:** add up all the income earned making those goods: wages, rent, interest, and profit. Every dollar spent is a dollar someone earns, so both methods should match.

sections.heading: Nominal vs. Real GDP
sections.markdown:
Suppose GDP goes up 5 percent. Did we make 5 percent more stuff, or did prices just go up 5 percent?
- **Nominal GDP** uses current prices. It can rise just because of inflation.
- **Real GDP** is adjusted for price changes. It shows whether we're actually producing more.
Economists care most about real GDP. To compare living standards between countries, they use **GDP per capita**: GDP divided by population. A huge country can have a huge GDP but a low GDP per capita.

sections.heading: What GDP Misses
sections.markdown:
GDP is useful, but it's not a happiness score. It doesn't measure:
- how income is shared (**income distribution**),
- leisure time,
- pollution or environmental damage,
- the value of volunteering and parents caring for kids at home,
- health, safety, or quality of life.
That's why economists also look at measures like life expectancy, education levels, and the **Human Development Index**.

sections.heading: Economic Growth
sections.markdown:
**Economic growth** means a steady increase in **real GDP per capita** over time. It's how standards of living rise. The average American today is many times richer than in 1900, with things nobody back then could imagine.
Growth comes from:
- **Physical capital:** more and better tools, machines, and buildings.
- **Human capital:** better-educated, healthier, more skilled workers.
- **Technology:** new ideas, from the steam engine to the internet to AI.
- **Natural resources:** used wisely.
- **Good institutions:** property rights, rule of law, stable government, and open markets give people incentives to invest and invent.
To grow, a country has to **save and invest** some of today's output instead of consuming it all. That's the PPC from Chapter 2 again: build more capital now and your whole curve shifts outward later.
Small growth rates add up. An economy growing 3 percent a year doubles in about 24 years (Rule of 72!). At 1 percent, it takes 72.

Then name one thing GDP leaves out that you think matters for people's well-being.

checklist: GDP = total market value of final goods and services made within a country in a year.
GDP = C + I + G + (X - M); consumption is the biggest piece.
Real GDP adjusts for inflation; GDP per capita compares living standards.
GDP leaves out used goods, unpaid work, pollution, leisure, and how income is shared.
Growth comes from capital, human capital, technology, resources, and good institutions.

title: Unemployment and Inflation

sections.heading: Two Ways the Trail Gets Rough
sections.markdown:
A healthy economy has two big goals besides growth: **jobs for people who want them** and **stable prices**. When either one goes wrong, families feel it fast.
Lose your job and the paychecks stop. Watch prices climb faster than your pay, and your paycheck shrinks even if the number on it stays the same.

sections.heading: Measuring Unemployment
sections.markdown:
The **unemployment rate** is the share of the **labor force** that doesn't have a job but is actively looking for one.
**Unemployment rate = (unemployed ÷ labor force) × 100**
The Bureau of Labor Statistics measures it every month by surveying about 60,000 households. Remember from Chapter 9: you're only in the labor force if you have a job or are looking. Retirees, full-time students not job hunting, and **discouraged workers** (people who've given up looking) aren't counted as unemployed. That's one reason the official rate can make things look better than they are. **Underemployed** workers (part-time but want full-time, or working below their skill level) aren't counted as unemployed either.
In a healthy U.S. economy, the unemployment rate is often around **4 to 5 percent**. In the worst month of the Great Depression it hit about 25 percent. In April 2020, during the pandemic, it spiked to almost 15 percent.

sections.heading: Four Types of Unemployment
sections.markdown:
- **Frictional:** people between jobs or just entering the workforce. A new grad searching for the right job. This is normal and even healthy.
- **Structural:** workers' skills don't match the jobs available, often because of new technology or industries moving. When a mine or mill closes, its workers may need retraining.
- **Seasonal:** jobs that come and go with the seasons. Ski instructors in summer, raft guides in winter, farm workers after harvest.
- **Cyclical:** job losses caused by a recession, when the whole economy slows down. This is the painful kind.
Because frictional and structural unemployment always exist, the unemployment rate never hits zero. **Full employment** means there's no cyclical unemployment. The leftover rate is called the **natural rate of unemployment**.

sections.heading: Inflation: When Prices Climb
sections.markdown:
**Inflation** is a general rise in prices across the economy over time. It means each dollar buys less. Your **purchasing power** shrinks.
**Deflation** is the opposite, a general fall in prices. It sounds nice, but it usually comes with collapsing businesses and job losses, like in the Great Depression.
**Hyperinflation** is inflation out of control. In Germany in 1923, prices doubled every few days and people carted bags of money to buy bread. Zimbabwe and Venezuela have had hyperinflation in recent decades.

sections.heading: Measuring Inflation: the CPI
sections.markdown:
The **Consumer Price Index (CPI)** tracks the price of a "**market basket**" of things a typical household buys: food, rent, gas, clothes, medical care, and more. The BLS checks thousands of prices every month.
The **inflation rate** is the percent change in the CPI from one year to the next. If the basket cost $100 last year and $104 this year, inflation is 4 percent.
The Federal Reserve aims for about **2 percent** inflation a year. A little inflation is considered normal. In 2022, U.S. inflation hit about 9 percent, the highest in 40 years, and you probably remember grocery and gas prices jumping. Since then it has come down but stayed above the Fed's 2 percent target.

sections.heading: What Causes Inflation?
sections.markdown:
- **Demand-pull inflation:** too much money chasing too few goods. When people and the government spend faster than the economy can produce, sellers raise prices.
- **Cost-push inflation:** costs of production jump (oil prices, wages, supply chain problems), and businesses pass those higher costs on to customers.
- **Too much money:** if the money supply grows much faster than the economy's output, each dollar is worth less. Printing money to pay bills is how most hyperinflations start.
Sometimes inflation feeds itself in a **wage-price spiral**: prices rise, workers demand raises, businesses raise prices to pay for the raises, and around it goes.

sections.heading: Who Wins and Who Loses?
sections.markdown:
Inflation hurts:
- **Savers**, if their interest rate is lower than inflation. 1 percent interest with 4 percent inflation means you're losing purchasing power.
- **People on fixed incomes**, like some retirees.
- **Lenders**, who get paid back in dollars worth less.
Inflation can help **borrowers** with fixed-rate loans, since they repay with cheaper dollars.
That's why economists separate **nominal** values (in today's dollars) from **real** values (adjusted for inflation). If you get a 3 percent raise but inflation is 5 percent, your **real wage** fell by about 2 percent.

2. Your summer job gave you a 4 percent raise, but inflation was 6 percent. Did your **real wage** go up or down? By about how much? Explain what that means for what you can buy.
3. Give one example each of **frictional, structural, seasonal,** and **cyclical** unemployment from Idaho.

checklist: Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labor force × 100.
Four types: frictional, structural, seasonal, cyclical; full employment means no cyclical unemployment.
Inflation = prices rising and purchasing power falling; the CPI measures it.
The Fed targets about 2 percent inflation.
Inflation hurts savers and fixed incomes and can help borrowers; real = adjusted for inflation.

title: The Business Cycle: Booms and Busts

sections.heading: Up the Ridge, Down the Saddle
sections.markdown:
No trail climbs straight up forever. It rises to a peak, dips into a saddle, then climbs again. The economy does the same thing. Over the long run, the U.S. economy grows. But along the way it speeds up and slows down in waves.
Economists call those waves the **business cycle**.

sections.heading: The Four Phases
sections.markdown:
1. **Expansion:** real GDP is growing. Businesses hire, unemployment falls, people spend more, and confidence is high. Expansions can last for years. The longest in U.S. history ran almost 11 years, from 2009 to 2020.
2. **Peak:** the top of the wave. The economy is running at full speed, sometimes so hot that inflation starts climbing.
3. **Contraction:** real GDP shrinks. Businesses cut back, layoffs rise, and people spend less. If the decline is serious and widespread, it's a **recession**. A common rule of thumb is two quarters (six months) in a row of falling real GDP, though the official call in the U.S. is made by economists at the National Bureau of Economic Research, who look at jobs, income, sales, and production too.
4. **Trough:** the bottom. Things stop getting worse, and recovery begins. A new expansion starts.
A very long, very deep recession is a **depression**. The U.S. has had only one big one in modern history.

sections.heading: What Moves the Cycle?
sections.markdown:
Economists have several explanations, and real cycles usually involve more than one:
- **Business investment:** when businesses feel good, they build factories and buy equipment, which creates jobs. When they get nervous, they stop, and the slowdown spreads.
- **Consumer confidence:** worried people spend less. Less spending means fewer sales, which means layoffs, which makes people more worried. Expectations can become self-fulfilling.
- **Interest rates and credit:** cheap borrowing fuels spending and investment. When rates rise or banks stop lending, spending drops.
- **External shocks:** surprise events like wars, pandemics, oil price spikes, and natural disasters.
- **Technology and industrialization:** big new technologies can launch long booms. They can also cause bubbles when people get carried away.

sections.heading: Wars, Factories, and Technology
sections.markdown:
History shows big forces shaping the cycle.
- **Industrialization:** in the late 1800s, railroads, steel, and factories caused rapid growth, but also wild swings. **Financial panics** in 1873 and 1893 led to deep slumps. Idaho's mining and railroad towns boomed and busted along with them.
- **Wars:** **World War II** pulled the U.S. out of the Great Depression. Government spending on tanks, planes, and ships put millions to work, and unemployment fell from double digits to under 2 percent. Wars can also cause inflation (too much spending, too few consumer goods) and recessions when spending suddenly stops after the war ends.
- **Technology:** the computer and internet boom of the 1990s brought a long expansion, then the **dot-com bubble** burst in 2000 when overhyped internet stocks crashed.

sections.heading: Three Famous Busts
sections.markdown:
**The Great Depression (1929-1941).** The stock market crashed in October 1929. Thousands of banks failed (remember bank runs from Chapter 10?), spending collapsed, and unemployment hit about 25 percent. Idaho farmers saw crop prices crash so low that some let crops rot in the fields. The Depression led to big changes, including the FDIC, Social Security, and a bigger government role in the economy.
**The Great Recession (2007-2009).** Banks made risky home loans to people who couldn't repay them. When home prices fell, those loans went bad, big financial firms collapsed, and credit froze. About 8.7 million jobs disappeared. Boise-area home values dropped sharply. The government responded with bank rescues, spending, and very low interest rates.
**The COVID-19 Recession (2020).** The shortest recession on record, about two months, but one of the sharpest. Businesses shut down to stop the virus, and unemployment spiked to almost 15 percent in April 2020. Huge government relief spending and low interest rates fueled a fast rebound, and then high inflation in 2021 and 2022.

sections.heading: Predicting the Weather
sections.markdown:
Economists watch **economic indicators** to spot where the cycle is heading, like a hiker watching clouds.
- **Leading indicators** change *before* the economy does: stock prices, new building permits, new orders for factory goods, the average workweek, and consumer confidence surveys.
- **Coincident indicators** move *with* the economy: employment, personal income, industrial production.
- **Lagging indicators** change *after*: the unemployment rate and inflation often keep moving even after the economy has turned.
Even with all this data, forecasting is hard. In Unit 7 you'll see how government and the Federal Reserve try to smooth out the cycle, so the dips aren't as deep and the peaks don't overheat.

A recession is a widespread decline in economic activity; a depression is a long, severe one.
Investment, confidence, interest rates, shocks, and technology move the cycle.

Leading indicators change before the economy; lagging indicators change after.

title: Taxes: Who Pays and What For

sections.heading: Who Plows the Road?
sections.markdown:
Somebody plows the snow off Highway 20 at 4 a.m. Somebody pays the teachers in your school, staffs the fire station, and maintains the trailhead parking lot at Craters of the Moon.
Most of that is paid for with **taxes**: required payments from people and businesses to the government. Taxes are the price of the shared services we use every day.

sections.heading: Principles of Taxation
sections.markdown:
People argue about taxes constantly, but most agree a good tax should be:
- **Fair (equity):** people should pay their fair share. (What's "fair" is the big debate.)
- **Simple:** easy to understand and pay.
- **Efficient:** easy and cheap to collect, without distorting choices too much.
Two ideas about fairness:
- **Benefits-received principle:** people who use a service should pay for it. Gas taxes pay for roads, and drivers are the ones buying gas.
- **Ability-to-pay principle:** people who earn more should pay more, because they can afford it.

sections.heading: Three Tax Structures
sections.markdown:
Taxes are grouped by how they hit people at different income levels.
- **Progressive tax:** the higher your income, the higher the *percentage* you pay. The **federal income tax** is progressive. It uses **tax brackets**: the first slice of income is taxed at 10 percent, the next slice at 12 percent, and so on up to 37 percent on very high incomes. Only the dollars inside each bracket get that bracket's rate.
- **Proportional (flat) tax:** everyone pays the same percentage. **Idaho's income tax** is flat: **5.3 percent** of taxable income for everyone (as of 2026).
- **Regressive tax:** takes a bigger *share* of income from lower-income people, even though the rate is the same. **Sales tax** is usually regressive. A $1,000 TV costs everyone $60 in Idaho sales tax, but $60 is a much bigger chunk of a $20,000 income than a $200,000 one.

sections.heading: Federal Taxes
sections.markdown:
The federal government's biggest sources of money:
1. **Individual income tax**: the largest source, roughly half of federal revenue. You file a **tax return** (Form 1040) each year by **April 15**. Your employer withholds tax from each paycheck based on your **W-4**; at the end of the year you get a **W-2** showing what you earned and what was withheld. If too much was withheld, you get a **refund**. Too little, you owe.
2. **Payroll taxes (FICA)**: 6.2 percent for Social Security and 1.45 percent for Medicare, with employers matching it.
3. **Corporate income tax**: 21 percent on company profits.
4. Smaller sources: **excise taxes** on specific goods like gasoline, alcohol, and tobacco; **tariffs** on imports; and the **estate tax** on very large inheritances.
Most people don't pay tax on every dollar they earn. The **standard deduction** lets you subtract a set amount before figuring tax, and **tax credits** subtract straight from what you owe.

sections.heading: State and Local Taxes in Idaho
sections.markdown:
Idaho pays for its services mostly with three taxes:
- **Sales tax:** 6 percent statewide, on most goods, including groceries. Some resort towns like Sun Valley and McCall add a small local tax. To offset the grocery tax, Idaho gives residents a **food tax credit**: $155 per person, or up to $250 if you save your grocery receipts. Sales tax is Idaho's single biggest source of state and local tax money.
- **Income tax:** the flat 5.3 percent.
- **Property tax:** a yearly tax on the value of homes, land, and businesses, paid to **counties, cities, and school districts**. It's the main way local governments pay for schools, roads, police, and fire departments. School districts also ask voters to approve **levies** and **bonds** for buildings and programs, so voters directly decide some local taxes.
Other taxes you'll see: Idaho's **gas tax** (33 cents a gallon, used for roads), vehicle registration fees, and taxes on hotel stays and tobacco.

sections.heading: How Taxes Affect You
sections.markdown:
Taxes shape decisions:
- **Personal finance:** taxes are a big expense in your budget. Your net pay, the price you pay at the register, and the cost of owning a home all include taxes. A house in a county with higher property taxes costs more each year.
- **Incentives:** taxes on things like tobacco discourage use. Tax breaks for retirement accounts encourage saving. Taxes that are too high can discourage work or investment, which is why people debate tax rates so hard.
- **Public services:** you get things back for your taxes: roads, schools, parks, public safety, clean water, and programs for people who are elderly, disabled, or in need.
The **tax incidence** asks who *really* pays a tax. A tax charged to a business may be passed on to customers through higher prices or to workers through lower wages.

3. Idaho uses a **flat** income tax, while the federal income tax is **progressive**. Which do you think is fairer, and which **principle of taxation** supports your view?

checklist: Good taxes aim to be fair, simple, and efficient.
Progressive (federal income tax), proportional/flat (Idaho income tax, 5.3%), regressive (sales tax).
Federal money comes mostly from income and payroll taxes; file by April 15.
Idaho relies on sales tax (6%), income tax, and local property tax, with a $155 food tax credit.
Taxes change prices, incentives, and your budget, and they pay for shared services.

title: Government Spending, Fiscal Policy, and the National Debt

sections.heading: Following the Money
sections.markdown: Chapter 19 showed where government money comes from. Now let's see where it goes, and how government uses spending and taxes to steer the whole economy.

sections.heading: Where Federal Money Goes
sections.markdown:
The federal government spends more than $7 trillion a year. The biggest pieces:
- **Social Security**: monthly checks for retirees, disabled workers, and survivors. The single largest program.
- **Health care**: **Medicare** (people 65+) and **Medicaid** (low-income families, shared with states).
- **National defense**: the military.
- **Interest on the national debt**: now more than $1 trillion a year, bigger than the defense budget.
- Everything else: veterans' benefits, food assistance, highways, education aid, national parks, science, and more.
Economists split this into two kinds:
- **Mandatory spending** is set by existing laws and happens automatically, like Social Security and Medicare. It's most of the budget.
- **Discretionary spending** is decided each year by Congress, like defense, education, and parks.
Some spending is **transfer payments**: money moved from taxpayers to individuals without buying a good or service, like Social Security checks and unemployment benefits.

sections.heading: State and Local Spending
sections.markdown:
Idaho's state budget is very different. Its biggest item is **K-12 public schools**, then **health and human services** (including Medicaid), then **colleges**, **prisons and public safety**, and **transportation**. Local governments spend on schools, roads, police, fire, parks, and water.
One big difference: **Idaho's constitution requires a balanced budget**. The state can't spend more than it takes in each year. The federal government has no such rule.

sections.heading: Deficits and Debt
sections.markdown:
- A **budget deficit** happens when the government spends more than it collects in a year.
- A **budget surplus** is the opposite: more revenue than spending. The federal government last ran a surplus in 2001.
- The **national debt** is all the past deficits added up (minus surpluses): the total the federal government owes.
To cover deficits, the Treasury **borrows** by selling bonds (Chapter 12) to Americans, banks, pension funds, foreign governments, and even the Federal Reserve.
The national debt passed **$40 trillion** in 2026. That's more than the whole economy produces in a year.
Why does debt matter?
- **Interest costs** grow and crowd out other spending.
- Heavy government borrowing can push up interest rates for everyone, which may reduce business investment. Economists call this **crowding out**.
- Future taxpayers, which means you, inherit the bill.
- But borrowing can make sense for emergencies (wars, recessions, pandemics) and investments that pay off over decades, like highways or research.
Economists and politicians disagree about how big a problem the debt is and how to fix it. The basic choices are raising taxes, cutting spending, growing the economy faster, or some mix. Every option has trade-offs and real people on the other side.

sections.heading: Fiscal Policy: Steering With Spending and Taxes
sections.markdown:
**Fiscal policy** is Congress and the President using **government spending** and **taxes** to influence the economy. (It's "fiscal" because it's about the government's budget.)
**Expansionary fiscal policy**: used in a recession to boost the economy.
- Increase government spending (projects, aid).
- Cut taxes so people and businesses have more to spend.
- Goal: more spending, more jobs, faster growth.
- Risk: bigger deficits, and if overdone, inflation.
**Contractionary fiscal policy**: used when the economy is overheating with high inflation.
- Cut government spending.
- Raise taxes.
- Goal: cool demand and slow inflation.
- Risk: it's unpopular, and it can slow growth or cause job losses.
The economist **John Maynard Keynes** argued government should spend more during recessions to make up for weak private demand. That's the idea behind most expansionary policy. Others argue that tax cuts and lighter regulation work better, by giving people and businesses stronger incentives to work, save, and invest. That's often called **supply-side** economics.
Examples: in 2009 and again in 2020, Congress passed huge spending and relief bills to fight recessions. Big tax-cut bills, such as those in 2017 and 2025, are fiscal policy too.

sections.heading: Automatic Stabilizers and Time Lags
sections.markdown:
Some fiscal policy happens on autopilot. **Automatic stabilizers** kick in without Congress voting:
- In a recession, more people collect **unemployment insurance** and food assistance, which keeps spending from collapsing.
- Income tax collections fall when incomes fall, leaving people more money.
Planned fiscal policy is slow. Congress has to notice the problem, debate, pass a law, and then the money has to reach people. By the time it arrives, the economy may have already changed. That's called a **time lag**, and it's one reason the Federal Reserve (next chapter) often moves first.

1. Recommend an **expansionary fiscal policy**: one spending change or one tax change. Explain how it should help using the words **demand** and **jobs**.
2. Name one **trade-off** or risk of your plan, and explain how it connects to the **national debt**.

checklist: The biggest federal spending: Social Security, health care, defense, and interest on the debt.
Mandatory spending happens automatically; discretionary spending is set by Congress each year.
Deficit = spending more than revenue in a year; the national debt is all past deficits added up (over $40 trillion).
Fiscal policy uses spending and taxes: expansionary in recessions, contractionary against inflation.
Automatic stabilizers work without new laws; planned fiscal policy has time lags.

title: The Federal Reserve and Monetary Policy

sections.heading: The Thermostat for Money
sections.markdown:
Your cabin has a thermostat. Too cold, turn up the heat. Too hot, turn it down. The economy has a thermostat too, and it's run by the **Federal Reserve**.
When the economy's sluggish, the Fed tries to warm it up. When it's overheating with inflation, the Fed cools it down. It does that mostly by changing how expensive it is to borrow money.

sections.heading: What Is the Fed?
sections.markdown:
The **Federal Reserve System** (the **Fed**) is the **central bank** of the United States. Congress created it in **1913** after a string of banking panics.
It's built in three layers:
- The **Board of Governors** in Washington, D.C.: seven members appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate for 14-year terms. One is the **chair**, who is often called the second most powerful person in Washington.
- **Twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks** around the country. Idaho is in the **12th District**, served by the **Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco**, which has a branch in Salt Lake City.
- The **Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC)**: the Board plus five regional bank presidents. They meet eight times a year to set monetary policy.
The Fed is designed to be **independent**. Its decisions don't need approval from Congress or the President. The idea is to keep short-term politics (like an upcoming election) from pushing it to make choices that feel good now but cause inflation later. That independence is sometimes controversial, and presidents have occasionally pressured Fed leaders publicly.

sections.heading: The Fed's Jobs
sections.markdown:
1. **Monetary policy:** managing the money supply and interest rates.
2. **Supervising banks:** making sure banks are safe and follow the rules.
3. **Lender of last resort:** lending to banks in an emergency so a panic doesn't spread.
4. **Running the payment system:** clearing checks and electronic payments, and distributing currency. (The Treasury's Bureau of Engraving and Printing actually prints the bills; the Fed puts them into circulation.)
5. **Banker to the government:** the U.S. Treasury keeps its account at the Fed.
Congress gave the Fed a **dual mandate**: aim for **maximum employment** and **stable prices**. In practice, "stable prices" means about **2 percent inflation** (Chapter 17).

sections.heading: Monetary Policy Tools
sections.markdown:
**Monetary policy** is the Fed changing the money supply and interest rates to influence the economy.
The Fed's main target is the **federal funds rate**: the interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. It ripples out to almost every other rate: car loans, credit cards, mortgages, and savings accounts. In fall 2026, the Fed's target range was **3.75 to 4 percent**.
The Fed moves it with these tools:
- **Interest on reserves:** the Fed pays banks interest on the money they keep at the Fed. Raise that rate, and banks won't lend to others for less. This is now the Fed's main tool.
- **Open market operations:** buying and selling government bonds. When the Fed **buys** bonds, it pays with new money, adding to the money supply and pushing rates down. When it **sells** bonds, money flows out and rates rise.
- **The discount rate:** the rate the Fed charges banks that borrow directly from it.
- **Reserve requirements:** the share of deposits banks must keep in reserve. (The Fed set this to zero in 2020 and relies on the other tools now.)

sections.heading: Easy Money and Tight Money
sections.markdown:
**Expansionary (easy-money) policy**: used in a recession.
- Lower interest rates, add money to the economy.
- Borrowing gets cheaper, so people buy cars and houses and businesses invest.
- More spending means more jobs.
- Risk: if kept too long, it can cause inflation or bubbles.
**Contractionary (tight-money) policy**: used to fight inflation.
- Raise interest rates, pull money out.
- Borrowing gets expensive, spending slows, and price growth cools.
- Risk: if overdone, it can trigger a recession.
Real examples: in 2008 and 2020, the Fed cut rates to nearly zero and bought trillions of dollars in bonds to fight recessions. In 2022 and 2023, it raised rates quickly, its fastest hikes in 40 years, to bring down 9 percent inflation. That's why mortgage rates jumped and home sales slowed.

sections.heading: Fed vs. Congress: Comparing the Tools
sections.markdown:
- **Who:** fiscal is Congress and the President; monetary is the Federal Reserve.
- **Tools:** fiscal uses spending and taxes; monetary uses interest rates and the money supply.
- **Speed:** the Fed can change rates in a single meeting, while Congress can take months. But both take time to work through the economy.
- **Politics:** fiscal policy is decided by elected officials; the Fed is designed to be independent.
They work best when they pull in the same direction. When they don't, say, Congress spending heavily while the Fed tries to slow inflation, they can work against each other.

2. Explain how your decision would affect a family trying to buy a house and a business deciding whether to build a new factory.
3. Why might it matter that the Fed is **independent** from the President and Congress?

checklist: The Fed is the U.S. central bank, created in 1913; Idaho is in the 12th District (San Francisco).
Dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices (about 2% inflation).
The FOMC targets the federal funds rate using interest on reserves, open market operations, and the discount rate.
Easy money = lower rates to fight recessions; tight money = higher rates to fight inflation.
Fiscal policy = Congress and taxes/spending; monetary policy = the Fed and interest rates/money.

title: Why We Trade: Specialization and Comparative Advantage

sections.heading: Your Breakfast Went Around the World
sections.markdown:
Look at your morning. Your phone was designed in California and assembled in Asia from parts made in a dozen countries. Your banana came from Ecuador. Your hoodie was sewn in Bangladesh. Your coffee? Colombia or Ethiopia. And the fries at lunch might be made from Idaho potatoes.
Nobody, and no country, makes everything for itself. Trade is how we get far more than we could ever produce alone.

sections.heading: Why Trade at All?
sections.markdown:
Remember **voluntary exchange** from Chapter 3: people only trade when both sides expect to be better off. The same is true between countries.
**Imports** are goods and services bought from other countries. **Exports** are goods and services sold to other countries.
Trade lets countries:
- get things they can't make at all (Idaho can't grow bananas or coffee),
- get things more cheaply than they could make them,
- sell to billions of customers instead of just their own,
- **specialize** in what they do best and become more productive.

sections.heading: Absolute Advantage
sections.markdown:
A country has an **absolute advantage** when it can produce more of something than another country using the same resources. If Idaho farmers can grow more potatoes per acre than farmers in another state, Idaho has an absolute advantage in potatoes.
That idea, from Adam Smith, explains some trade. But it misses a surprising truth.

sections.heading: Comparative Advantage: The Big Idea
sections.markdown:
What if one country is better at making *everything*? Should it still trade? Yes. Here's why.
A country has a **comparative advantage** when it can produce something at a **lower opportunity cost** than another country. Economist **David Ricardo** explained this in 1817.
Try it with two people. Jordan and Sam are building a campsite.
- In one hour, **Jordan** can either gather **10 bundles of firewood** or set up **5 tents**.
- In one hour, **Sam** can either gather **4 bundles of firewood** or set up **4 tents**.
Jordan is faster at both. Jordan has the absolute advantage in both. But look at opportunity costs:
- For Jordan, 1 tent costs 2 bundles of firewood (10 ÷ 5).
- For Sam, 1 tent costs only 1 bundle of firewood (4 ÷ 4).
Sam gives up less to set up a tent. So **Sam has the comparative advantage in tents**, and **Jordan has the comparative advantage in firewood**. If Jordan gathers wood and Sam sets up tents, together they get more done than if each tried to do both. Both win.
That's the magic of comparative advantage: **every country has a comparative advantage in something**, and specializing and trading lets everyone have more.

sections.heading: Specialization in the Real World
sections.markdown:
Countries specialize based on their resources, climate, skills, and technology.
- **Idaho** specializes in potatoes, dairy and cheese, trout, sugar beets, hops, barley, and wheat, plus computer chips, lumber, and food processing.
- **Brazil:** coffee, soybeans, and orange juice.
- **Saudi Arabia:** oil.
- **Taiwan:** advanced computer chips.
- **Germany:** cars and machinery.
Specialization makes countries **interdependent**: they rely on each other. That's efficient, but it also means a problem in one place can ripple everywhere. In 2021, a shortage of computer chips from Asia shut down car factories in the U.S. because modern cars need dozens of chips.

sections.heading: Entrepreneurs and Trade
sections.markdown:
Trade isn't just countries. It's businesses and entrepreneurs finding customers worldwide. Successful businesses use the same idea: they specialize in what they do best and trade for the rest. A small Idaho trout farm might sell fish to restaurants across the country, a Boise software startup might sell to customers in Japan, and a potato processor in Burley might ship frozen fries to Asia.
Successful entrepreneurs in a global economy:
- find their **comparative advantage** (what they can do better or cheaper than others),
- use **specialization** inside the business (Chapter 2's division of labor),
- reach far-off markets through the internet, shipping, and trade agreements,
- watch for risks like changing exchange rates and trade rules (Chapter 23).

sections.heading: Gains and Pains
sections.markdown:
Trade makes countries richer overall, with lower prices and more variety for consumers. Exporting industries add jobs. Competition pushes businesses to improve.
But the gains aren't spread evenly. When imports are cheaper, some domestic industries shrink and workers lose jobs. Many U.S. factory towns lost jobs as manufacturing moved overseas. That's real pain for real families, which is why trade is one of the most debated topics in politics. Programs like job retraining try to help workers move to new industries. You'll see the policy fights in the next chapter.

1. Who has the **absolute advantage** in potatoes? In chips?
2. Calculate each one's **opportunity cost** of 1 chip. Who has the **comparative advantage** in chips? In potatoes?
3. What should each specialize in, and why does trading make both better off?

checklist: Imports are bought from other countries; exports are sold to them.
Absolute advantage = can produce more; comparative advantage = lower opportunity cost.
Every country has a comparative advantage in something, so specializing and trading helps both sides.
Specialization makes countries interdependent, for better and worse.
Trade raises overall wealth, but some workers and industries lose.

title: Trade Policy and Exchange Rates

sections.heading: Who Opens the Gate?
sections.markdown:
Trade crosses borders, and borders have gates. Governments decide how wide to open them. Some want the gate wide open: **free trade**. Others want to close it partway to protect workers and businesses at home: **protectionism**.
This is one of the oldest fights in economics, and it's still front-page news.

sections.heading: Barriers to Trade
sections.markdown:
Governments limit trade with a few main tools:
- **Tariff:** a tax on imported goods. A 25 percent tariff on imported steel makes foreign steel cost more, so U.S. steel looks cheaper by comparison. The **importer** pays the tariff to the U.S. government, and much of that cost is usually passed on to buyers through higher prices.
- **Quota:** a limit on how much of a product can be imported.
- **Embargo:** a ban on trade with a country, usually for political reasons. The U.S. has had an embargo on Cuba since the early 1960s.
- **Subsidies:** government payments to domestic producers so they can sell more cheaply at home or abroad.
- **Rules and standards:** safety, labeling, or environmental rules that can make it harder for foreign goods to enter.

sections.heading: The Case for Protection
sections.markdown:
Supporters of protectionism argue:
- **Protecting jobs:** cheaper imports can wipe out domestic industries and the towns that depend on them.
- **National security:** a country shouldn't depend on rivals for critical things like steel, medicine, energy, and computer chips.
- **Infant industries:** new industries may need protection until they're strong enough to compete.
- **Fair play:** some countries break the rules by heavily subsidizing their companies or **dumping** products (selling below cost to drive competitors out).

sections.heading: The Case for Free Trade
sections.markdown:
Supporters of free trade argue:
- **Lower prices and more choices** for consumers. Tariffs work like a tax on shoppers.
- **Comparative advantage** (Chapter 22): specializing and trading makes everyone richer overall.
- **Export jobs:** U.S. farmers and manufacturers sell to the world. Idaho exports billions of dollars of goods each year, especially computer chips, food, and farm products.
- **Retaliation risk:** if the U.S. places tariffs, other countries often fire back with tariffs on U.S. goods. Idaho potato, dairy, and wheat farmers have been hit by retaliatory tariffs in past trade disputes.
Most economists favor freer trade, while recognizing that some workers and communities are hurt and need help adjusting. Voters and politicians in both major parties are split on how much protection is right, and U.S. tariff policy has swung back and forth in recent years.

sections.heading: Trade Agreements
sections.markdown:
Countries make deals to lower trade barriers.
- **USMCA** (United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, 2020), which replaced **NAFTA** (1994). Canada and Mexico are among Idaho's biggest trading partners.
- The **World Trade Organization (WTO)** sets rules for trade among more than 160 member countries and settles disputes.
- **Free trade zones** and agreements with individual countries lower tariffs between partners.
- The **European Union** goes further: its members trade freely, and most share a common currency, the **euro**.

sections.heading: Balance of Trade
sections.markdown:
A country's **balance of trade** is its exports minus its imports.
- **Trade surplus:** exports are bigger than imports.
- **Trade deficit:** imports are bigger than exports.
The U.S. has run a trade deficit almost every year since the 1970s. Is that bad? Economists debate it. A deficit means Americans are buying lots of foreign goods, but it also means foreigners are sending money back to invest in the U.S., buying American stocks, bonds, and businesses. A deficit isn't automatically a sign of a weak economy.

sections.heading: Exchange Rates
sections.markdown:
To trade, you usually have to swap currencies. An Idaho company selling cheese to Japan gets paid in Japanese **yen**, then trades them for dollars. The **exchange rate** is the price of one currency in terms of another.
Exchange rates change every day based on supply and demand for each currency. This is a **floating exchange rate**.
- A **strong dollar** (it buys more foreign currency) makes **imports cheaper** for Americans and makes trips abroad cheaper. But it makes **U.S. exports more expensive** for foreigners, which hurts Idaho farmers and manufacturers selling overseas.
- A **weak dollar** does the opposite: exports get cheaper for foreign buyers and imports get more expensive for Americans.
Example: if $1 = 150 yen, a $10 pound of Idaho cheese costs a Japanese buyer 1,500 yen. If the dollar strengthens to $1 = 200 yen, the same cheese costs 2,000 yen, and Japanese shoppers may buy less.

thinkLikeAScientist.prompt:
The U.S. places a 25 percent tariff on imported bicycles.
1. Explain how the tariff affects (a) American shoppers, (b) a U.S. bike factory, and (c) Idaho farmers if the other country **retaliates** with tariffs on U.S. potatoes.
2. Do you support the tariff? Use one argument from **each side** of the free trade vs. protectionism debate, then explain which one you find stronger.

checklist: Trade barriers: tariffs, quotas, embargoes, subsidies, and rules.
Protectionism argues for jobs, national security, and infant industries; free trade argues for lower prices, comparative advantage, and export jobs.
Trade agreements like USMCA and the WTO lower barriers.
Balance of trade = exports - imports; the U.S. usually has a trade deficit.
A strong dollar makes imports cheaper and exports more expensive; a weak dollar does the reverse.

title: The Global Economy and Idaho

sections.heading: The View From the Summit
sections.markdown:
You made it. From the top of a peak in the Sawtooths, you can see range after range in every direction. Every one connects to the others through valleys, rivers, and passes.
That's the **global economy**: every country connected to every other through trade, money, people, and ideas. What happens in a factory in China, an oil field in the Middle East, or a bank in London can change prices in Idaho Falls by next week.

sections.heading: Globalization
sections.markdown:
**Globalization** is the growing connection of the world's economies. Several things sped it up:
- **Transportation:** giant container ships, cargo planes, and the humble **shipping container** (invented in the 1950s) cut the cost of moving goods around the world dramatically.
- **Communication:** the internet and smartphones let a business in Boise work with partners on the other side of the planet in real time.
- **Trade agreements** lowered tariffs (Chapter 23).
- **Global finance:** money moves across borders in seconds, so investors can buy stocks and bonds anywhere.
Businesses now use **global supply chains**: a product is designed in one country, built from parts made in several others, and sold everywhere. **Multinational corporations** operate in many countries at once.
Globalization has helped lift billions of people out of extreme poverty. The World Bank estimates the share of the world living in extreme poverty fell from more than a third in 1990 to under 10 percent in recent years. But it also brings competition for jobs, worries about workers' rights and the environment, and the risk that a crisis in one place spreads everywhere.

sections.heading: Developed and Developing Countries
sections.markdown:
Countries are often grouped by income and living standards.
- **Developed countries** (like the U.S., Canada, Japan, Germany) have high GDP per capita, strong industries, good education and health care, and stable institutions.
- **Developing countries** have lower incomes, more people working in agriculture, and less access to education, clean water, and health care. Many are growing fast. **Emerging economies** like India, Indonesia, and Vietnam are shifting quickly toward industry and services.
What helps a country develop? The same growth ingredients from Chapter 16:
- **Human capital:** education and health.
- **Physical capital and infrastructure:** roads, power, internet, ports.
- **Stable institutions:** property rights, the rule of law, and low corruption.
- **Open trade** and investment from abroad.
**Foreign aid** (grants and loans from richer countries) and organizations like the **World Bank** (loans for development projects) and the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** (helps countries in financial crisis) try to support development. **Microloans** give tiny loans to entrepreneurs in poor areas so they can start small businesses.

sections.heading: Interdependence: When One Domino Falls
sections.markdown:
Because economies are linked, shocks travel.
- **Oil prices:** a war or a cut in production by OPEC raises gas prices everywhere, including at your local station.
- **Financial crises:** the 2008 U.S. housing crisis spread into a worldwide recession.
- **Pandemics:** COVID-19 shut factories in Asia, which emptied shelves in America.
- **Supply chain snarls:** in 2021, backed-up ports and a chip shortage delayed everything from cars to game consoles.
Countries **compete** too: for factories, investment, talent, and customers. Nations race to lead in technologies like computer chips, artificial intelligence, and clean energy. Governments sometimes use subsidies and tariffs to win that race, which can lead to trade tensions.

sections.heading: Idaho in the World
sections.markdown:
Idaho isn't on the sidelines. It's on the map.
- **Exports:** Idaho sells billions of dollars of goods abroad each year. The biggest export is usually **computer chips and electronics**, led by Boise-based **Micron Technology**. Food and farm products follow: frozen potatoes and fries, cheese and dairy, wheat, and other crops. Top destinations include Canada, Mexico, and countries across Asia.
- **Agriculture:** Idaho grows about a third of America's potatoes, ranks among the top dairy states, and leads the nation in farmed trout. Foreign buyers' tastes, exchange rates, and tariffs directly affect Idaho farm income.
- **Investment:** foreign companies build and buy in Idaho, and Idaho companies invest abroad. Micron has operations around the world and is building major new chip plants in Boise.
- **Imports:** Idahoans buy cars, phones, clothes, and countless other things made overseas, at prices that would be much higher without trade.
- **Tourism:** visitors from around the world come to Yellowstone, the Sawtooths, and Sun Valley, and spend money in Idaho businesses.
So when you hear about a tariff fight, a strong dollar, or a slowdown in China, ask: **what does this mean for Idaho?** Often, quite a lot.

sections.heading: Your Place in It
sections.markdown:
You'll compete for jobs in a global economy and buy from a global marketplace. The best preparation is the same advice from the whole course: build your **human capital**, make choices with **opportunity cost** in mind, manage your money with a **budget**, protect your **credit**, and let **compound interest** work for you.
That's the summit. Enjoy the view, then pick your next mountain.
